questions.question:
A Facilities team wants to manage building-access requests that involve badge provisioning, physical-security approval, and space-capacity checks. A Business Analyst has drafted process maps and conducted stakeholder interviews.
What does the team evaluate next to determine whether ServiceNow is the right platform for this solution?
options: Whether the core process aligns with platform capabilities for workflow, approvals, and SLA management
Whether Flow Designer subflows can orchestrate the physical-security approval without custom script includes
Whether a working prototype in App Engine Studio satisfies stakeholder expectations before architecture review
Whether a gap analysis of OOTB Facilities modules covers badge - provisioning field requirements
questions.explanation:
The team evaluates whether the core process aligns with platform capabilities. ServiceNow's architecture is purpose-built for task-based workflows, structured approvals, and service level agreement (SLA)-driven tracking. When process maps already show approval routing, sequenced fulfillment, and measurable timelines, these map directly to native platform capabilities. Confirming this alignment before evaluating specific modules or prototyping ensures the platform decision is justified by architectural fit, not premature solutioning.
The team does not perform a gap analysis of out-of-the-box (OOTB) Facilities modules as the next step. This skips the fundamental platform-fit question. Gap analysis assumes ServiceNow is already the right platform and jumps directly to feature-level evaluation of individual module capabilities. Feature evaluation without platform-fit validation risks committing to a platform that may not suit the process fundamentally.
The team does not evaluate Flow Designer subflows for physical-security approval as the next step. This is a detailed implementation question that presupposes platform selection. The team should first validate that the overall process type aligns with ServiceNow's core strengths before examining specific orchestration tools. Answering automation mechanics before confirming platform fit inverts the proper decision sequence and risks investing design effort in tooling details when the platform itself may not be the right choice for the underlying process requirements.
The team does not build a working prototype in App Engine Studio as the next step. Prototyping before confirming platform fit risks significant throwaway effort. Prototyping is appropriate after the team establishes that ServiceNow's architecture matches the process requirements. Creating a prototype before validating platform alignment can bias the decision toward ServiceNow regardless of whether the fit is actually strong, because stakeholders may anchor on the visible prototype rather than objectively evaluating whether the platform's core capabilities truly match the process needs.
questions.reference: Determine if an application is a good fit with ServiceNow

questions.question:
HR requests a new scoped application to track employee certifications. Discovery shows that HR Service Delivery already covers most of the requirements.
What is the recommended first step before the team approves custom development?
options: Conduct a documented fit-gap assessment against HR Service Delivery
Deliver a lightweight custom application based on HR Service Delivery
Clone the HR Service Delivery data into a custom table model
Build a parallel scoped application that uses HR Service Delivery as a template
questions.explanation:
The recommended first step is a documented fit-gap assessment against Human Resources (HR) Service Delivery. Because the existing product already covers most of the requirements, the assessment identifies which needs the product meets through configuration and which gaps remain. Custom development, if any, then targets only those gaps and preserves the upgrade path of the existing product.
Building a parallel scoped application duplicates capabilities that HR Service Delivery already provides. The team would maintain two data models for the same process, and reporting would be split across both applications.
Delivering a lightweight custom application spends development effort before the team knows whether the existing product meets the need. If HR Service Delivery covers the requirement, the custom work is discarded.
Cloning HR Service Delivery data into custom tables separates the data from the product's business logic, reporting, and upgrades. Every behavior that the product provides would have to be rebuilt and maintained in the custom tables.
questions.reference: Determine if an application is a good fit with ServiceNow

questions.question:
A department needs governed repositories of information with approval workflows, role-based access, and search. They want to avoid custom development.
Which platform capability does the department use?
options: Knowledge Management with article workflows and user-criteria visibility
HR Service Delivery with document management and employee portal publishing
Customer Service Management with self-service knowledge base integration
Service Catalog with knowledge-type catalog items and variable-driven content
questions.explanation:
The department uses Knowledge Management. Knowledge Management natively provides article lifecycle workflows, user-criteria-based visibility controls, and full-text search. These capabilities directly address all three stated requirements without custom development. Evaluating the purpose-built solution before considering alternatives or custom builds follows configuration-first principles and avoids duplicating functionality that already exists on the platform. Knowledge Management also integrates with Service Portal and Employee Center for self-service access, and supports versioning and feedback collection out of the box.
The department should not use Service Catalog. Service Catalog it is designed for request fulfillment, not article management. Catalog items capture structured requests and route them through approval and fulfillment workflows. Using catalog variables to store article content misapplies the catalog's purpose and would require significant customization to replicate the article lifecycle, categorization, and search features that Knowledge Management provides natively. Catalog items also lack versioning, user-criteria visibility controls, and content authoring workflows.
The department should not use Customer Service Management (CSM). It is designed for external customer-facing service delivery, not internal article governance. Using CSM for internal governed articles introduces unnecessary product complexity and licensing considerations. CSM brings customer-specific entities such as accounts, contacts, and entitlements that are irrelevant to an internal article governance use case.
The department should not use HR Service Delivery (HRSD). Its document management capabilities are designed specifically for HR content such as policies and employee onboarding materials. Using HRSD for general internal article management extends the product beyond its intended scope and introduces HR-specific workflows, portal structures, and lifecycle templates that do not align with a general article governance requirement.

questions.question:
A legal department stores contract records on an existing custom table and needs a two-stage approval with a complete history of field changes. A Developer proposes a new scoped application to meet these needs.
Which factor argues against the proposal?
options: Scoped applications are unable to run approval flows on tables outside their scope.
The existing table already supports Flow Designer approval actions and table auditing.
New scoped applications require a published Store listing before they use approval actions.
Two-stage approvals are available only on tables that extend the Task table.
questions.explanation:
The existing table already supports both requirements. Workflow Studio (Flow Designer) approval actions can request approvals on records of any table, and auditing can be enabled for the table to record field changes with the user and time of each change. Fields can be excluded from or limited to an audit through dictionary attributes. A new application would duplicate the data model without adding a capability.
Scoped applications can run approval flows on tables in other scopes when the target table's Application Access settings allow the required operations. Scope does not prevent the approval process.
Approval actions are available to an application as soon as it is created. Publishing to the ServiceNow Store is a distribution step for other instances and is unrelated to using platform features on the development instance.
Approval actions are available for any table. Tables that extend Task provide additional approval fields and related lists, but extending Task is a convenience, not a requirement for approvals.
questions.reference: Determine if an application is a good fit with ServiceNow

questions.question:
A business unit asks for custom fields and scripts in Global to speed delivery. The Architect expects long-term ownership by multiple teams.
Which approach does the Architect follow?
options: Build in a private scoped application
Develop in the current scope and normalize scope later
Split logic across Global and private scopes
Implement the requested changes in Global
questions.explanation:
Building in a private scoped application is most appropriate because scoped apps provide namespace isolation, portability, and governed access to platform resources. Scope boundaries prevent naming collisions and unintended side effects when multiple teams contribute. Private scope also enables distribution through the ServiceNow Store or update sets with clear ownership boundaries. Application Access settings on each table give administrators fine-grained control over which external scopes can read, write, or extend artifacts owned by the application.
Implementing the requested changes directly in Global is not the most appropriate approach. Global scope artifacts lack namespace isolation, making naming collisions and unintended interactions likely as multiple teams contribute. Global customizations are harder to package for distribution and cannot be protected against modification on target instances. Long-term governance is significantly harder without scope boundaries. Global artifacts also cannot leverage Application Access controls or protection policies, so any Administrator with sufficient role access can modify Business Rules, Script Includes, and other components without restriction.
Developing in the current scope and normalizing scope later is not the most appropriate approach. Scope assignment is effectively permanent after artifacts are created. Migrating artifacts between scopes requires recreation of tables, scripts, and configurations, since scope namespace is embedded in every artifact identifier at creation time. Planning the correct scope from the beginning avoids costly rework. Table names, Script Include API names, and property keys all carry the scope prefix, so changing scope means rebuilding every artifact and updating all cross-references.
Splitting logic across Global and private scopes is not the most appropriate approach. This creates fragmented ownership and complicates dependency management. Cross-scope calls between Global and private scope introduce access-control complexity and make packaging and distribution unreliable. A single private scope keeps all artifacts under one governance model. When logic spans scopes, update set migration requires careful sequencing to avoid broken references, and troubleshooting runtime errors becomes harder because execution crosses scope boundaries with different access rules and logging contexts.
questions.reference: Determine if an application is a good fit with ServiceNow

questions.question: Which platform capability allows a team to capture structured requests, route multi-level approvals, and trigger task generation without custom development?
options: A UI Builder page with form components and client-side task creation
A portal widget with custom form submission and scripted approval routing
Record Producer with direct table insertion and manual assignment
Service Catalog with catalog item workflows and fulfillment automation
questions.explanation:
Service Catalog provides the complete request-to-fulfillment pipeline: catalog items capture structured input, approval workflows route requests through defined approval chains, and fulfillment tasks are generated automatically upon approval. This matches all three stated requirements without custom development. Catalog items also support variable sets for reusable form components, execution plans for multi-task fulfillment, and integration with Service Portal for self-service submission.
Record Producer does not inherently include approval routing or automated fulfillment task generation. Record Producer handles only request capture. While Record Producers can be placed inside the catalog, standalone Record Producers lack the request-item lifecycle and catalog task framework needed for structured fulfillment.
A portal widget will not reduce the need for custom building. Recommending custom scripting as an alternative to a custom application does not achieve the goal of evaluating out-of-the-box (OOTB) capabilities before committing to development effort. Custom widgets also require ongoing maintenance through platform upgrades and introduce client-side code that must be independently tested, secured, and documented outside the standard catalog framework.
A UI Builder page does not provide server-side approval routing or automated fulfillment logic. Client-side task creation bypasses the governance controls that server-side approval workflows enforce. Client-side record creation also skips Business Rule evaluation order guarantees and may circumvent ACL protections if the API calls are not properly secured with appropriate scope and role checks.

questions.question:
A developer opens Schema Map and tries to create a new child table from the relationship diagram. The option is unavailable.
Which feature of Schema Map explains this behavior?
options: It requires users with `security_admin` role.
It is a visualization tool.
It allows table creation only in Global scopes.
It requires a table-design plugin.
questions.explanation:
Schema Map is a visualization tool that provides a graphical view of table relationships, fields, and hierarchy for analysis purposes. It does not support creating, modifying, or deleting tables or fields. Developers must use Table Designer, the sys_db_object form, or Studio to perform schema modifications. Schema Map is strictly a read-only reference for understanding existing data model structure and exploring parent-child table inheritance chains visually.
Schema Map does not allow table creation in Global scopes. The read-only restriction applies universally regardless of application scope context. Whether the developer is working in Global or a private scoped application, Schema Map provides the same visualization-only functionality without any creation or modification capabilities.
Schema Map does not require the [security_admin] role for table creation. This role controls access to ACL definitions and security-related configurations, not schema design tools. Schema Map visibility is governed by standard administrative roles, but no role unlocks creation features because the tool is exclusively for visualization. Table creation is performed through Table Designer or the sys_db_object form, where the appropriate admin role grants access to those separate creation interfaces.
Schema Map does not require a table-design plugin. No plugin activation changes Schema Map from read-only to editable. The platform provides separate tools such as Table Designer specifically for table creation and modification, which are distinct from Schema Map's visualization purpose. Schema Map is available on base platform instances without additional plugin activation, and its read-only nature is an intentional design constraint to prevent accidental schema changes while exploring data model relationships.
questions.reference: Design and implement a data model

questions.question:
A Developer creates the Facilities Request [x_acme_fac_request] table, which extends the Task table. Users then create several Facilities Request records.
Which statement describes how these records relate to the Task table?
options: The records belong to the Task table hierarchy and appear in Task lists with Facilities Request as their class.
The records are copied to the Task table by a scheduled synchronization job.
The records appear in Task lists only after a database view joins the two tables.
The records are stored only in the child table and are excluded from Task lists.
questions.explanation:
When a table extends another table, its records belong to the parent table's hierarchy. A query or list on the Task table returns Facilities Request records together with records of other task types, and the Class [sys_class_name] field identifies each record as a Facilities Request. The child records also have the fields defined on the Task table.
No synchronization job is involved. The Task table uses the table-per-hierarchy extension model, in which one database table stores the records of Task and of all its child classes, so nothing is copied.
Records of a child table are part of the parent table hierarchy. Excluding them from Task lists would defeat the purpose of extending Task, which is to reuse its fields and processes.
A database view is used to join tables that are not related through extension. Extended tables need no view because the parent table already includes the child records.
questions.reference: Design and implement a data model

questions.question:
An onBefore Business Rule is defined on a parent table. New records inserted on a child table trigger the parent's Business Rule.
What explains this behavior?
options: Parent business rules propagate when the rule's Table field expands to include child tables.
Parent business rules are copied to child tables during the table creation process.
Parent business rules run on child tables if `advanced=true` is set on the child table.
Parent business rules execute for child-table records unless conditions exclude them.
questions.explanation:
Parent business rules execute for child-table records unless conditions exclude them. Table inheritance in ServiceNow means scripts defined on a parent table apply to all child tables automatically at runtime. The rules are not copied; they fire live from the parent definition whenever a qualifying operation occurs on any descendant table. To prevent unwanted execution, the Business Rule condition must explicitly filter out child tables using a condition such as `current.sys_class_name == 'parent_table'` to restrict execution to only the parent table itself.
Parent business rules are not copied to child tables. Inheritance is a runtime behavior, not a one-time duplication event. The parent rule's single definition fires dynamically against any table in the hierarchy, so there is no separate copy on the child table that could be independently modified or deleted. Updating the parent rule immediately affects all child tables without propagation, and child tables cannot opt out without a condition change on the parent rule.
Parent business rules do not run on child tables if `advanced=true` is set on the child table. The Advanced checkbox on a Business Rule enables the script editor for that specific rule; it has no relationship to table inheritance behavior. Parent rules fire on child tables regardless of this flag. The Advanced setting determines whether the Business Rule form displays the script field and condition scripts, or restricts the form to the simplified filter-based condition interface.
Parent Business Rules do not propagate when the rule's Table field expands to include child tables. Inheritance is a runtime behavior, not a metadata change. It remains set to the parent table only. The system evaluates the table lineage during each database operation, not by modifying the Business Rule record. No metadata on the rule changes when a child table is created. The class hierarchy resolver determines at runtime whether the current record's table is a descendant and fires the rule accordingly.
questions.reference: Design and implement a data model

questions.question:
A Developer needs to model one request linked to multiple skills, and one skill linked to multiple requests, without duplicating values across records.
Which design pattern does the Developer use?
options: Store links in a journal field and parse entries at runtime for relationship lookups
Create an explicit many-to-many table with two reference fields
Create reference fields on both tables and keep them synchronized in Business Rules
Add a long string field on each table that stores comma-separated foreign `sys_id` values
questions.explanation:
The Developer creates an explicit many-to-many table with two reference fields. This approach models the bidirectional relationship without data duplication. The intermediary table stores one record per relationship, with each record holding a reference to the request and a reference to the skill. This is the standard ServiceNow approach for many-to-many relationships. The platform uses this pattern internally for constructs like user-group membership, where the sys_user_grmember table links users and groups through paired reference fields.
The Developer does not add a long string field storing comma-separated sys_id values. This approach breaks referential integrity, cannot be indexed or queried efficiently, and requires custom parsing logic. The platform has no built-in support for enforcing or resolving relationships stored as delimited strings, making this approach fragile and non-standard. Delimited strings also impose a field-length limit on the number of relationships and prevent the use of related lists for navigating the relationship from either side.
The Developer does not create reference fields on both tables and keep them synchronized in Business Rules. This approach introduces unnecessary complexity and a risk of data inconsistency. If synchronization logic fails or executes out of order, the relationship data becomes unreliable. The many-to-many table pattern eliminates this synchronization requirement entirely. A single reference field on each table can hold only one sys_id value, so it cannot represent a one-to-many relationship without delimited strings or multiple fields, neither of which is a supported relational pattern.
The Developer does not store links in a journal field and parse entries at runtime for relationship lookups. Journal fields are designed for timestamped text entries such as work notes and comments, not structured relational data. Runtime parsing of journal content for relationship lookups is unreliable, unindexable, and cannot leverage platform relationship features such as related lists, dot-walking, or reference qualifiers. Journal entries are also append-only and timestamped, making updates and deletions of individual relationship links impractical.
questions.reference: Design and implement a data model

questions.question:
A developer writes a script that passes gr.getValue('requested_for') into an email notification body to display the requester's name. The output shows a 32-character hexadecimal string instead.
What explains this behavior?
options: Reference fields store `sys_id`.
Reference fields store the display value and resolve the sys_id at query time.
The field type was changed to Encrypted Text, which returns a hashed token on read.
getValue() returns a label when the dictionary cache is stale.
questions.explanation:
Reference fields store the target record's sys_id as the column value, not the display name. The requested_for field is a reference to the User table, so getValue() retrieves the stored 32-character sys_id. To obtain the human-readable name for the notification, the developer uses getDisplayValue() on that field, which resolves the display value from the referenced record. Alternatively, dot-walking through the reference (such as gr.requested_for.name) retrieves field values from the referenced record directly, though this triggers an additional database query.
Reference fields do not store the display value and resolve the sys_id at query time. The platform stores the raw sys_id as the database column value and resolves display values on demand through the reference relationship. When a form renders a reference field, the platform looks up the display value using the stored sys_id, but the underlying column contains only the 32-character identifier. The resolution direction is sys_id to display value, not the reverse.
The dictionary cache stores metadata about field definitions such as type, max length, and attributes. It does not alter the runtime return value of getValue(), which reads the raw column data from the database record. A stale dictionary cache can affect field label rendering or form layout, but it has no effect on what getValue() returns for a reference field - the result is always the stored sys_id regardless of cache state.
Encrypted Text fields produce variable-length encrypted strings that differ from the fixed 32-character hexadecimal format of a sys_id. The 32-character output in this scenario is consistent with standard reference field behavior, not encryption. Encrypted Text values require the platform's decryption context to read and are not human-readable even when decrypted to their original form, whereas a sys_id is a plaintext GUID.
questions.reference: Design and implement a data model

questions.question:
In a private scoped app, a Developer creates a table named `asset_registry`.
What is the default naming behavior for the physical table?
options: ServiceNow prefixes it with the app namespace.
ServiceNow stores custom table names in uppercase.
ServiceNow requires custom tables to begin with `sys_`.
ServiceNow adds a `u_` prefix.
questions.explanation:
ServiceNow prefixes the table with the app namespace because scoped applications enforce namespace isolation. A table created as `asset_registry` in a private scope with namespace `x_vendor_app` becomes `x_vendor_app_asset_registry` as the physical table name. This automatic prefixing prevents naming collisions between applications and ensures every artifact is uniquely identifiable by its owning scope. The namespace prefix also applies to Script Includes, system properties, and scheduled jobs, maintaining consistent scope identification across artifact types.
ServiceNow does not add a `u_` prefix to scoped application tables. The `u_` prefix convention applies only to custom fields and tables created in Global scope. Scoped applications use the scope's namespace prefix instead, which provides vendor-specific isolation rather than the generic `u_` prefix used for unscoped customizations. The `u_` prefix identifies artifacts as user-created Global customizations, while the `x_` prefix indicates a scoped application artifact with its vendor and app identifiers embedded in the namespace.
ServiceNow does not store custom table names in uppercase. Table names are stored in their original case as defined during creation, with the namespace prefix prepended. The platform uses case-sensitive table naming internally, and there is no uppercase conversion behavior for custom or scoped table identifiers. Table names in ServiceNow follow lowercase conventions by default, and the platform expects consistent casing when referencing tables in scripts, GlideRecord queries, and REST API endpoints throughout the instance.
ServiceNow does not require custom tables to begin with `sys_`. `sys_` is reserved for platform system tables that ship with the base instance. The platform enforces this reservation to prevent custom artifacts from conflicting with system tables, ensuring that platform upgrades can introduce new system tables without overwriting customer-created objects.
questions.reference: Design and implement a data model

questions.question: Which action resolves a module record with valid arguments and roles failing to appear in the application navigator?
options: Set the correct module order
Add the module to the table's Related Links configuration
Set the Link type to Separator
Associate the module to an Application Menu
questions.explanation:
Associating the module to an Application Menu is the most direct fi. Modules require a parent menu container to render in the navigator. The Application Menu defines the navigation group, and without this association the platform has no location to render the module. Restoring the menu association makes the module visible to users with appropriate roles. The menu controls the collapsible section header, so a module without a menu parent has no section to display under.
Setting the correct module order does not fix the issue. The Order field controls display sequence within a menu, not whether the module appears at all. Order only takes effect once the module is properly parented to a menu. Lower Order values position the module higher in the menu's list, but this sequencing is meaningless if the module has no parent menu.
Adding the module to the table's Related Links configuration does not fix the issue. Related Links are contextual shortcuts on forms, not navigator entries. They have no effect on navigator rendering or module visibility, which is governed by the menu association and role configuration. Related Links provide quick access to related records or functions through UI Actions or form design, but they operate within the form interface, not the application navigator.
Setting the Link type to Separator does not fix the issue. Separator is a visual divider that creates spacing in the navigator but does not link to content. A separator module will not provide access to the intended target. Even if the separator rendered, it produces a non-clickable line between modules and does not navigate to any table, URL, or content page.
questions.reference: Create modules

questions.question:
A team wants a navigator module that opens the Incident table showing only records where Active is true and Region is EMEA without using custom scripting.
Which module link type does the team use?
options: List of Records
Content Page
URL link
Map Page
questions.explanation:
List of Records is the most appropriate link type because it is purpose-built for opening a table's list view with an encoded query filter applied. The Developer specifies the target table and enters the encoded query string (in this case, `active=true^region=EMEA`) in the Filter field, and the platform renders a standard list with the conditions pre-applied. This approach requires zero scripting and integrates with all native list features including column sorting, grouping, breadcrumbs, and list controls. List of Records is the standard module link type for filtered table navigation throughout the platform.
URL link is not the most appropriate. It constructs a literal URL from the Arguments field and navigates to a raw address. While a Developer could manually build a `/now/nav/ui/classic/params/target/table_list.do?sysparm_query=...` URL, this approach bypasses the platform's native module-to-list integration and produces a brittle configuration that can break if URL structures change across platform versions. List of Records achieves the same result declaratively without requiring the developer to construct or maintain URL syntax. URL (from arguments) is designed for linking to external pages or non-standard internal resources that lack a dedicated link type.
Content Page is not the most appropriate. Content Page renders a named Content Management System (CMS) content page within the navigator frame, not a table view with conditions applied. Content Pages are part of the legacy CMS and display authored HTML or wiki content. They have no built-in mechanism for specifying a target table, applying an encoded query filter, or rendering a standard list view with native platform list controls. Using a Content Page to display a filtered record list would require building a custom page that manually embeds a list component, defeating the requirement to avoid custom scripting.
Map Page is not the most appropriate. It renders a geographic map interface, not a standard table view with query conditions. Map Pages are used for location-based visualizations and require map-specific configuration such as map source and location fields. They do not support encoded query filters in the same way List of Records does, and they present data spatially rather than in a tabular list format. The requirement specifies opening a filtered list, which is a tabular display concern that Map Page is not designed to address.
questions.reference: Create modules

questions.question:
Facilities agents need a navigator entry that opens a blank Facilities Request form so that they can create a request directly from the application menu.
Which module link type does the Developer select?
options: Content Page
List of Records
Single Record
New Record
questions.explanation:
The New Record link type opens a form for a new record on the table that the module specifies. Agents select the module and complete the blank Facilities Request form.
The List of Records link type opens a list view of the table, optionally filtered. Agents would have to select New from the list to reach a blank form.
The Single Record link type opens one existing record that the module identifies. It does not open a blank form for a new record.
The Content Page link type opens a page from the Content Management System (CMS). It does not open a table form.
questions.reference: Create modules

questions.question:
Users have the role required by a module, but the module is still hidden from them in the application navigator.
Which statement explains this behavior?
options: ACL checks on target tables are evaluated before navigator role checks.
Application Menu role checks are evaluated first.
User criteria on modules replace menu-level role evaluation.
Module role checks override parent menu restrictions by default.
questions.explanation:
The application navigator checks the roles of the Application Menu before it checks the roles of its modules. Users who lack the menu role see none of its modules, even when they have the module role. The exception is a module with Override application menu roles selected, which is visible to users who have the module role.
Module roles do not override the menu roles by default. A module bypasses the menu role check only when Override application menu roles is selected on the module.
Access control lists (ACLs) control access to records and fields after a user opens the module. They do not determine whether a module appears in the application navigator.
Modules do not support user criteria. Navigator visibility is controlled by the roles on the application menu and the module, and by the Override application menu roles option.
questions.reference: Create modules

questions.question:
The app menu requires admin, but one specific navigation entry needs to be exposed to itil users without granting admin.
Which setting enables this exception?
options: Set a Condition field on the module that evaluates the user's role list at render time
Duplicate the app menu and maintain separate role trees
Enable `Override application menu roles` on the Application Menu record
Enable `Override application menu roles` on the module
questions.explanation:
Enabling `Override application menu roles` on the module allows it to bypass the parent menu's role requirement and use its own role configuration instead. This means itil users can see this specific module without needing the admin role that the Application Menu requires, providing granular access control at the module level. The override affects only the individual module where it is enabled; all other modules under the same Application Menu continue to require the admin role.
Enabling `Override application menu roles` on the Application Menu record does not achieve the desired result. The override setting is a module-level property, not a menu-level property. The Application Menu record defines the menu-level role requirement that applies to all child modules by default, but the override checkbox exists on the module form for individual exceptions. Configuring the override on the wrong record level has no effect on module visibility.
A Condition field on the module does not bypass the parent menu's role requirement. The hierarchical role evaluation happens before any module-level condition is checked. Without the override flag, the menu-level role requirement blocks the module regardless of condition logic. Module conditions filter records within the target list, such as filtering by assignment group, but they do not control module visibility.
Duplicating the app menu does not enable the exception. This approach requires managing two parallel menu structures with overlapping content, which increases the risk of configuration drift and makes future changes harder to coordinate. Any new module added to one menu must be replicated in the other, and role changes must be synchronized.
questions.reference: Create modules

questions.question:
A Developer in Scope A creates an application menu named Facilities. A colleague in Scope B creates modules for the same process and expects them to appear under the Facilities menu automatically. The modules appear under a different menu.
Which statement explains this behavior?
options: Each module appears under the application menu with the highest order value.
Each module appears under the application menu referenced in its Application menu field.
Each module appears under the application menu that belongs to the same scope as the module.
Each module appears under the application menu that was created most recently.
questions.explanation:
A module appears in the navigator under the application menu selected in its Application menu field. Creating a menu in another scope does not move existing modules into it. To place the Scope B modules under Facilities, the colleague selects the Facilities menu in each module's Application menu field.
Modules are not grouped by scope. A module can reference an application menu that belongs to another scope; for example, scoped applications often add modules to existing platform menus.
The Order field controls the position of menus and modules in the navigator. It does not determine which menu a module belongs to.
Creation date has no effect on where a module appears. The Application menu field on the module defines its parent menu.
questions.reference: Create modules

questions.question: Which UI control switches the active scope?
options: System Properties > Application settings
User preferences
Application Picker
Update Set picker
questions.explanation:
The Application Picker in the header is used to switch active scope. When a Developer creates tables, scripts, or other artifacts, they are assigned to the scope currently selected in the Application Picker. Switching the picker immediately redirects all subsequent artifact creation to the intended scope. The Application Picker is a session-level control visible in the banner frame that persists across navigation until explicitly changed.
System Properties > Application settings does not control active scope selection. System properties control instance-wide configuration values, not which scope the Developer is currently working in. System properties may exist within a specific scope, but navigating to property pages does not change which scope receives newly created tables, scripts, or other artifacts.
The Update Set picker does not switch active scope. It controls which update set captures configuration changes for migration. Update sets and application scope are independent concepts: an update set can capture changes from any scope, and switching update sets does not change the active application scope. The Update Set picker and Application Picker are separate header controls serving different purposes: one tracks changes for deployment, while the other determines artifact ownership.
User preferences does not switch active scope. It controls the initial page displayed after login, not the active application scope. Landing page configuration does not affect which scope the developer is working in or where newly created artifacts are assigned. User preferences include settings like time zone, date format, and notification options, but none of these preferences influence application scope context or artifact ownership during development activities on the instance.
questions.reference: Use Application scope

questions.question:
A Business Rule in Scope A calls a Script Include in Scope B. The Script Include has Accessible from set to All application scopes and queries a table that belongs to Scope B. The call is still blocked.
Which configuration explains this?
options: The Script Include has a Protected protection policy, which blocks calls from other scopes.
The Scope B table blocks Can read access from other application scopes.
The Script Include has Client callable cleared, which blocks calls from other scopes.
The Script Include restricts callers, and the request from Scope A is awaiting approval.
questions.explanation:
Accessible from makes the Script Include available to other scopes, but a resource can also restrict its callers. When the Script Include's caller access is set to Caller Restriction, a call from another scope creates a restricted caller access request that an administrator must set to Allowed before the call succeeds.
The Script Include runs in its own scope, Scope B. Its query on a Scope B table is a same-scope operation, so the table's Application Access settings, such as Can read, do not apply. These settings apply when code from another scope queries the table directly.
Client callable allows browser scripts to call the Script Include through GlideAjax. Server-side calls from other scopes do not require it.
Protection policies control whether users on a target instance can view or edit the Script Include code. They do not block runtime calls.
questions.reference: Use Application scope

questions.question:
A table in Scope B has `Allow configuration` enabled for all application scopes. A Developer in Scope A can add a field but still is unable to query records.
Which statement explains this behavior?
options: `Allow configuration` is ignored unless the table also extends `task`.
`Allow configuration` grants read access, while writes still require ACL permission.
`Allow configuration` permits structural changes, not implicit read/write data access.
`Allow configuration` and `Can read` are equivalent controls for cross-scope consumers.
questions.explanation:
`Allow configuration` permits structural changes such as adding fields, but it does not grant implicit read or write data access. These are separate permission controls in the Application Access settings. To query records from another scope, the table must also have `Can read` enabled. This separation allows Administrators to share schema extensibility without exposing record data.
`Allow configuration` does not grant read access. The distinction is between configuration access and data access, not between read access and write access. Configuration access and data access are independently controlled through separate checkboxes in Application Access settings. A scope can be permitted to modify table structure while being denied access to the data stored in that table. This separation lets table owners allow external scopes to add custom fields without exposing underlying record data.
`Allow configuration` and `Can read` are not equivalent controls. Configuration access controls schema modification, while `Can read` controls data query rights. They govern different aspects of cross-scope interaction: configuration access controls schema modification rights, while `Can read` controls data query rights. Treating them as equivalent would incorrectly imply that enabling one automatically enables the other. The Application Access record exposes these as separate checkboxes because table owners need granular control: extending the schema, reading data, writing data, or deleting data are each independently permissioned.
`Allow configuration` is not ignored unless the table extends `task`. This setting applies to any table regardless of its parent hierarchy. Whether a table extends task, cmdb_ci, or is a standalone root table, `Allow configuration` controls structural modification access from other scopes in the same way. Application Access settings are defined per table on the sys_scope_privilege record and are evaluated by the platform's scope manager at runtime independently of the table's inheritance chain or parent table configuration.
questions.reference: Use Application scope

questions.question: What happens if a team asks to rename a scoped app's prefix after months of development and committed artifacts?
options: Scope can be changed before first store publication.
Scope changes are handled by ServiceNow support on request.
Scope namespace is effectively set after creation.
Scope can be changed at any time in Application Manager.
questions.explanation:
Scope namespace is effectively set after creation. The scope prefix is embedded into every artifact name; tables, scripts, properties, and configuration records all reference the namespace. Renaming would require updating all internal references across the instance and external integrations. ServiceNow does not provide a bulk rename mechanism, making the namespace permanent once development begins. REST API endpoints, GlideRecord references, and Script Include API names incorporate the namespace, so a change would break integrations referencing these identifiers.
Scope cannot be changed at any time in Application Manager. The scope identifier is locked after initial creation. The Application Manager allows editing metadata such as display name and description, but the scope identifier is locked after initial creation. The scope field on the sys_app record is read-only after creation, and no administrative interface provides a mechanism to modify it.
Scope cannot be changed before first store publication. The namespace is set at application creation, not at publication time. Even during early development, artifacts like tables and scripts are created with the namespace prefix embedded in their identifiers. Waiting until publication does not provide a rename window. The first table or Script Include created immediately establishes dependencies on the namespace, so any rename after that would leave orphaned references throughout the application.
Scope changes are not handled by ServiceNow support on request. Namespace is architecturally embedded across all application artifacts. A namespace change would require recreating every table, field, script, and configuration record under the new prefix. This is effectively a full application rebuild, not a support-level configuration change. Data migration between the old and new tables would also be required, along with updating all ACLs, Business Rules, flows, and integrations that reference the original namespace-prefixed artifact names.
questions.reference: Use Application scope

questions.question: A REST API call from another scope fails to read records even though table Application Access has `Can read` enabled. Which missing table setting explains this behavior?
options: Add a cross-scope ACL rule granting REST operations on the table
Mark the table as extensible
Enable `Allow access to this table via web services`
Allow REST bypass using the `Allow configuration` option checkbox
questions.explanation:
Enabling `Allow access to this table via web services` is the missing setting that explains the behavior. This setting controls whether external API calls, including REST and SOAP, can interact with the table. `Can read` grants data query rights through application-scope logic such as Script Includes and Business Rules, but web service access requires its own separate permission flag. Web service calls originate from external systems and carry different security implications than internal scope-to-scope interactions.
Allowing REST bypass using the `Allow configuration` option checkbox is not the missing setting. This setting controls structural modification rights such as adding fields from other scopes, not web service access or API-level data query permissions. REST access requires its own dedicated checkbox in the Application Access settings.
Marking the table as extensible is not the missing setting. Table extensibility controls whether other scopes can create child tables, not whether REST API calls can query records. API access and table extension are independent aspects of Application Access configuration. Extensibility determines whether the table can serve as a parent in the class hierarchy for other applications, while web service access controls external API interactions.
Add a cross-scope ACL rule granting REST operations on the table is not the missing setting. ACLs govern record-level security, while Application Access controls cross-scope interactions including web service calls. Both layers must be satisfied for access to succeed, but this failure points to Application Access.
questions.reference: Use Application scope

questions.question:
Two planned apps both include a table logically named `request`.
Which platform feature prevents object-name collisions?
options: Each scoped app applies a unique namespace prefix to artifacts.
Custom objects can use one shared instance-wide prefix.
The second app is blocked from installation if names overlap.
Tables are auto-renamed with generated timestamp suffixes.
questions.explanation:
Each scoped app applies a unique namespace prefix to artifacts, which prevents object-name collisions. Two apps naming a table `request` produce physically distinct tables such as `x_vendorA_app_request` and `x_vendorB_app_request`. This namespace isolation ensures that independently developed applications can coexist on the same instance without object-name conflicts. The prefix is assigned during application creation and applies consistently to all artifact types including tables, Script Includes, system properties, and UI components within that scope.
The second app is not blocked from installation if names overlap. Each application's artifacts carry their own namespace, so logically identical names become physically distinct identifiers. There is no need for installation blocking because the naming architecture prevents collisions structurally. This design allows the ServiceNow Store to host multiple applications that use similar logical names without requiring publishers to coordinate naming conventions or verify name availability before publishing.
Tables are not auto-renamed with generated timestamp suffixes. The platform relies on deterministic namespace prefixes, not random or temporal suffixes, to ensure unique object names. Timestamp suffixes would create unpredictable and unreadable identifiers that complicate development and administration. Deterministic naming means developers can predict the full physical table name from the scope namespace and logical name, which is essential for writing scripts and referencing tables consistently across development, test, and production instances.
Custom objects cannot use one shared instance-wide prefix. A single prefix would not prevent collisions between applications. The purpose of namespace isolation is that each application receives a distinct prefix. A shared prefix would move the collision problem from the full table name to the portion after the prefix, defeating the purpose of namespacing. The three-part prefix (scope indicator, vendor identifier, and application name) ensures uniqueness across vendors and applications, providing collision prevention at every level.
questions.reference: Use Application scope

questions.question:
Support Managers need to see an extended form layout; however, they only see the Default view. The custom view exists and fields are configured.
What does the Developer do to address this issue?
options: Set the manager view as the table's default view for all users
Create a rule that correctly routes users to the intended form view
Add transform logic that maps role names to form section definitions
Create a UI Policy that switches users to the manager form view at runtime
questions.explanation:
The Developer creates a rule that correctly routes users to the intended form view. View Rules define conditions, typically based on user role, group membership, or other criteria, that determine which form view is displayed when a record is opened. Without a View Rule, the platform defaults to the Default view regardless of how many custom views have been configured. View Rules are evaluated in order and the first matching rule determines the view rendered for that user session.
The Developer does not add transform logic that maps role names to form section definitions. Transform maps are used for data import operations, not view selection. They process incoming records from external sources and have no relationship to how the platform selects which form view to display for a given user.
The Developer does not set the manager view as the table's default view for all users. A default view applies broadly when no specific routing rule matches, affecting all users rather than only support managers. The requirement is conditional targeting by role, which is handled by View Rules. View Rules evaluate user context and route matching users to the intended view while allowing other users to continue using the appropriate default or alternate view.
The Developer does not create a UI Policy to switch users to the Manager form view at runtime. UI Policies execute after the form is already loaded and can change field visibility, mandatory state, and read-only behavior, but they do not control which view the platform selected to render.
questions.reference: Create, design, and customize forms

questions.question: Which element displays instructional text between fields on a form, without new table columns or persisted data?
options: An annotation
A UI Macro
A system property
A String dictionary field
questions.explanation:
An annotation is a static display element that can be placed between fields on a form layout without creating a dictionary entry or database column. Annotations render text, labels, or formatting on the form surface purely for user guidance. No data is stored, and the annotation exists solely as a layout element on the configured form view. Annotations are configured through Form Layout or Form Designer by adding them to the desired position between fields on the form.
A String dictionary field adds a column to the underlying database table. Even if the field is set to read-only and populated with static text, it still consumes storage, appears in exports, and creates a schema element the team explicitly wants to avoid. Dictionary fields also require managing default values or Business Rules to populate the static text on every record, adding unnecessary maintenance overhead.
System properties store instance-level configuration values accessible through server-side APIs. They are not designed to display instructional text on forms between fields. While a property value could be referenced by scripts, it does not render as a form layout element positioned between specific fields. System properties are managed in the sys_properties table and serve configuration purposes such as controlling feature flags, default behaviors, and integration settings across the instance.
UI Macros are typically used for complex interactive elements, not simple instructional text between fields. Macros require development work and do not provide the same simple layout positioning that annotations offer for static text between specific fields. Additionally, header-level macros render at the top of the form rather than between specific fields.
questions.reference: Create, design, and customize forms

questions.question:
A Developer adds a reference from `u_project_task` to `u_project` and expects tasks to appear automatically on the project form. The related list fails to appear.
What does the Developer do to resolve this?
options: Rebuild the dictionary cache so the platform recognizes the new reference relationship
Add the appropriate related list to the project form layout
Configure a Data Policy that maps reference fields to form related lists
Define a transform map so the reference field can render as a related list
questions.explanation:
The Developer adds the appropriate related list to the project form layout. Creating a reference field establishes a data relationship but does not automatically modify the form layout of the referenced table. Related lists must be explicitly added to the target form through Form Layout or Form Designer. This is a manual configuration step that controls which relationships are displayed on the form.
The Developer does not rebuild the dictionary cache. Dictionary cache stores metadata about field definitions, but it does not control form layout rendering. A related list's visibility on a form is controlled by the form layout configuration, not by whether the reference field metadata has been cached. The related list will display data regardless of cache status once it is added to the layout.
The Developer does not configure a Data Policy to map reference fields to form related lists. Data Policies enforce field-level constraints such as mandatory and read-only behavior on records, including when accessed through APIs. They do not control which related lists appear on form layouts. Related list visibility is managed through the Form Layout slush bucket or Form Designer, where administrators explicitly select which related lists to display on a given form view.
The Developer does not define a transform map. Transform maps process incoming data during import operations, mapping source fields to target table fields. They have no role in form layout configuration or in determining which related lists appear when viewing a record. Transform maps are used with Import Sets to load data from external sources such as CSV files, JDBC connections, or LDAP directories, and they operate entirely outside the form rendering pipeline.
questions.reference: Create, design, and customize forms

questions.question:
A client UI Action in a scoped application needs record data before the onClick logic continues.
Which implementation follows the supported client/server pattern?
options: Enable table web services and run the GlideRecord query from onClick
Select Client and run the GlideRecord query inside the onClick function
Clear Isolate script and run the GlideRecord query from the form page
Use GlideAjax to call a Script Include that runs the GlideRecord query
questions.explanation:
Using GlideAjax to call a Script Include that runs the GlideRecord query follows the supported client/server pattern. The onClick function stays in the browser, where it can collect form context and make the request. The Script Include runs server-side code, so it is the right place to use GlideRecord for database work. This also matches ServiceNow guidance for scoped applications: use a Script Include with GlideAjax, or use REST APIs, instead of relying on client-side GlideRecord.
Selecting Client and running the GlideRecord query inside the onClick function leaves the database work in the browser-side script. The Client checkbox is useful when the UI Action needs an onClick function, but it does not make scoped client code a supported place for client-side GlideRecord. It simply changes the execution context to the browser. The database work still needs to move behind a supported bridge such as GlideAjax or REST.
Clearing Isolate script and running the GlideRecord query from the form page addresses a different client-side restriction. Script isolation limits access to page globals, direct DOM patterns, and older browser scripting habits. It is not the setting that makes client-side GlideRecord supported in a scoped application. Even with isolation changed, the record query still belongs in server-side code reached through GlideAjax or another supported server communication pattern.
Enabling table web services and running the GlideRecord query from onClick mixes an integration setting with a browser scripting problem. Web services access controls whether external clients can reach table data through interfaces such as REST or SOAP. It does not change the JavaScript API support available to a scoped client UI Action. The script still needs to request server-side record work through GlideAjax, REST, or another supported mechanism.
questions.reference: Create, design, and customize forms

questions.question: What makes a record page easier to scan and adds static inline guidance while preserving the existing table schema and field behavior?
options: Configuring a UI policy action
Configuring a data policy rule
Configuring a form section
Configuring a form annotation
questions.explanation:
Configuring a form section is the clean way to break a crowded record page into readable groups without creating a new field. Sections are part of the form layout: Administrators can add or reorder them and use one- or two-column layouts. That changes presentation, not the table model. Existing fields stay on the same table, and their required, read-only, or visibility rules do not need to change just because the page is easier to scan.
Configuring a form annotation adds static help text where users need context, without storing another value on the record. ServiceNow describes annotations as instructions or additional information about fields on a form, and the form designer lets administrators place annotation text in the layout. That makes them a good fit for inline guidance. The annotation is a display element, so it does not create a dictionary entry, database column, or field behavior rule.
Configuring a UI policy action can improve a form, but it is not the right fit when field behavior must stay unchanged. UI policies can make fields mandatory, read-only, visible, hidden, or cleared when conditions are met. Those are behavior changes for existing fields, not static organization or guidance. Even if no new table column is created, the requirement rules this out because the user experience changes through conditional field control.
Configuring a data policy rule is aimed at enforcing data consistency, not adding static organization or guidance to a page. Data policies set mandatory and read-only states and can apply beyond standard browser entry, including imports, web services, and mobile UI. That makes them useful when the same field rules must apply across entry points. It also means they change field behavior, while the requirement asks for a presentation-only change.
questions.reference: Create, design, and customize forms

questions.question:
A developer adds a new field to the Incident table using Table Builder. After saving, the field is missing on the Incident form.
What is the reason?
options: Publishing the application scope is required before Table Builder fields become available on forms
Using elevated administrative access is required before new fields appear on the Incident form
Adding a field to a table creates a dictionary entry, and the field still requires configuration in the form layout
Activating a new field in the dictionary is required before the field appears on any form
questions.explanation:
Adding a field to a table creates a dictionary entry; the field must also be added to the form layout separately. Table Builder and the dictionary define the data model, the columns and their properties, but form layouts are configured independently. A newly created field exists in the database and is accessible via scripts and APIs immediately after saving, but it will not appear on any form until a developer explicitly adds it to the desired form layout using Form Designer or the Form Layout editor. This two-step process keeps schema management and UI configuration separate, allowing the same field to be placed on multiple form views selectively.
Activating a new field in the dictionary is not required before the field appears on any form. When a field is created through Table Builder or the dictionary, it is active by default and available to the platform immediately. The Active flag on a dictionary entry controls whether the field is processed by the platform, but its default state upon creation is active. Activation status does not explain why a new field is absent from a form; the missing form layout configuration is the cause.
Publishing the application scope is not required before Table Builder fields become available on forms. Fields created in Table Builder are accessible within the instance immediately after saving, regardless of publication status. Publishing packages an application for distribution to other instances and has no bearing on whether fields are visible within the development instance where they were created.
Using elevated administrative access is not required before new fields appear on the Incident form. Adding a field to a table and configuring a form layout are standard developer tasks that fall within the typical application developer role. If insufficient access were the issue, the field creation step itself would have failed; the form layout and the dictionary are managed through separate, independent configurations.
questions.reference: Add/Remove fields from forms and tables

questions.question:
An administrator adds a new Region column to the Facilities Request list by using Configure > List Layout. Most users see the new column, but one user who previously changed the columns of that list still sees the old columns.
What does the user do to see the new column?
options: Request the personalize_list role from an administrator
Clear the browser cache and reload the list
Add the Region field to the default form view
Reset the personalized list to the column defaults
questions.explanation:
Configure > List Layout changes the default columns for all users. A user who personalized the list columns keeps the personal layout, so the user resets the personalized list to the column defaults to see the administrator's layout.
The personal column layout is stored as a user setting on the instance, not in the browser cache. Clearing the cache does not replace it.
The personalize_list role allows a user to configure list layouts for everyone. The user only needs to view the new default layout, so no additional role is needed.
Form views and list layouts are configured independently. Adding the field to a form has no effect on the columns of a list.
questions.reference: Add/Remove fields from forms and tables

questions.question: What does a Developer do to hide a field from a form but retain it in the schema for integrations and reports?
options: Set the field's Active dictionary attribute to false
Remove the element from the layout
Remove the element from list layout
Delete the dictionary entry
questions.explanation:
The Developer removes the element from the layout. This hides the field from the form's user interface without affecting the underlying dictionary entry or database column. Form layout controls which fields are visible on the form, and removing a field affects only form presentation. The field remains available for scripts, integrations, reports, and list views. This approach cleanly separates user-facing visibility from schema retention, allowing the field to continue serving backend purposes such as Business Rule logic, REST API responses, and scheduled report generation.
The developer does not delete the dictionary entry. Doing so removes the database column and destroys all existing data in that field. The Developer would also need to recreate the field again, which would produce an empty field with no historical data. This approach directly contradicts the requirement to retain the field in the schema for integrations and reports. Deleting a dictionary entry is a destructive operation that also breaks any existing Business Rules, Client Scripts, ACLs, reports, or integration mappings that reference the field. It should be used only when a field is being permanently retired from the data model.
The Developer does not set the field's Active attribute to false in the dictionary. While this might hide the field from some platform interfaces, the Active flag primarily controls whether configuration records are processed by the platform. For dictionary entries, deactivating can have unpredictable effects on scripts and integrations that reference the field.
The Developer does not remove the element from list layout. List layout and form layout are independent configurations. Removing from list layout would hide the field in tabular views while potentially leaving it visible on the form, which is the opposite of what is needed. List layout controls which columns appear when records are displayed in a list or table format, while form layout controls which fields appear when a single record is opened for viewing or editing.
questions.reference: Add/Remove fields from forms and tables

questions.question: When adding a new field to a table, which attributes are configured as part of initial field behavior?
options: Audit retention requirements
Table row-level ACL scripts
Length/size constraints
Data type and storage behavior
questions.explanation:
Data type and storage behavior is commonly configured during initial field setup. The data type determines how the platform stores, validates, and renders the field. Choosing between string, integer, reference, date/time, choice, or other types defines the field's core behavior and affects what values can be stored and how they interact with platform features. The data type also governs which input widgets are displayed on forms, which operators are available in queries and filters, and how the field participates in reporting and analytics.
Length and size constraints are dictionary-level attributes commonly configured at field creation. For string and text fields, the max length determines truncation behavior at write time. Setting appropriate constraints prevents data loss and ensures consistent data quality across integrations and user input. The default max length for a string field is 40 characters, which may be insufficient for many use cases and should be adjusted during initial configuration to match expected data requirements.
Table row-level ACL scripts are not configured as part of initial field behavior. ACLs are security rules configured separately from the dictionary and control access permissions at the record, field, or operation level. While ACLs reference fields and tables, they are independent security artifacts, not attributes of the field's dictionary definition. ACLs are managed through the Access Control table and evaluated at runtime when users attempt to read, write, create, or delete records. They are part of the security model, not the data model that is configured during initial field creation.
Audit retention requirements are not configured as part of initial field behavior. Auditing is configured at the table or field level through audit settings and retention policies, which are separate from the dictionary entry's core attributes like data type, length, and default value. Audit configuration determines which field changes are tracked in the sys_audit table and how long audit records are retained before archiving. These are operational governance decisions typically made after initial field creation and managed independently from the dictionary entry.
questions.reference: Add/Remove fields from forms and tables

questions.question:
A Developer needs fields that link records in one table to records in another table.
Which two field types are designed for table-to-table relationships?
options: Integer
String
List
Reference
questions.explanation:
A Reference field stores the sys_id of one record in a target table. It supports dot-walking, display values, and reference qualifiers, and the related records can be shown in related lists.
A List (glide_list) field stores the sys_ids of several records in a target table in one field. It links a record to multiple records in another table. It does not enforce referential integrity: if a referenced record is deleted, its sys_id can remain in the field.
A String field stores text. A value typed into it has no link to another table, so the platform cannot dot-walk through it or resolve display values.
An Integer field stores numbers. It has no reference to another table and provides no relationship features.
questions.reference: Add/Remove fields from forms and tables

questions.question: Why does a Developer who calls `g_form.setMandatory()` inside a Business Rule sees no UI change on the form?
options: `g_form` methods run after GlideRecord queries complete.
Business Rules can call `g_form` when the table extends `task`.
`g_form` is available only in client-side context.
`g_form` methods execute when the Business Rule runs in the `display` context.
questions.explanation:
`g_form` is available only in client-side context. Business Rules execute on the server where the `g_form` object does not exist. Server-side scripts cannot manipulate the form UI directly through `g_form`. To set field mandatory behavior from server-side logic, the Developer should use `g_scratchpad` with a Display Business Rule or dictionary-level mandatory configuration.
Business Rules cannot call `g_form` when the table extends `task`. Table inheritance does not affect API availability between client and server execution contexts. `g_form` is a client-side API regardless of which table is being used. The parent table hierarchy has no bearing on whether server-side scripts can access browser-based form manipulation objects. The task table hierarchy governs field inheritance, Business Rule inheritance, and ACL inheritance.
`g_form` methods do not run after GlideRecord queries complete. `g_form` and `GlideRecord` operate in different execution contexts: `g_form` runs in the browser and `GlideRecord` runs on the server. There is no sequential relationship between GlideRecord query completion and `g_form` method availability. They are independent APIs in separate runtime environments. Server-side scripts complete execution before the form is rendered in the browser, so there is no mechanism for a Business Rule to interact with `g_form` at any point during its execution lifecycle.
`g_form` methods do not execute when the Business Rule runs in the `display` context. While Display Business Rules execute during form loading, they still run on the server side. The `g_form` object is only available in actual client-side scripts like Client Scripts and UI Policies that execute in the browser. Display Business Rules can use `g_scratchpad` to pass data to client scripts, which then use `g_form` to manipulate the form. This two-step pattern is the correct way to influence form behavior from server-side logic.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug client-side scripts for desktop

questions.question:
A client script appends `g_form.addInfoMessage()` during repeated field changes. Users see duplicate banners stacking on the form.
How does a Developer resolve this?
options: Clear existing form messages before adding new ones
Move message rendering to Background Scripts
Replace `addInfoMessage()` with `addErrorMessage()`
Move the logic to an onSubmit Client Script
questions.explanation:
Clearing existing form messages before adding new ones avoids accumulation. Without calling `g_form.clearMessages()` first, repeated field changes cause multiple identical banners to stack on the form. Clearing before adding ensures only the current, relevant message is displayed to the user. The typical pattern is to call `g_form.clearMessages()` at the start of the onChange function and then call `g_form.addInfoMessage()` with the appropriate message text.
Moving message rendering to Background Scripts does not solve the accumulation issue. Background Scripts execute asynchronously on the server and have no access to the client-side form Document Object Model (DOM). They cannot render form banners or clear existing messages. Form message management must be handled in client-side context where `g_form` is available. Background Scripts are designed for administrative server-side tasks such as data cleanup, bulk updates, and diagnostic queries, not for interactive user interface operations that require real-time browser communication.
Replacing `g_form.addInfoMessage()` with `g_form.addErrorMessage()` does not solve the accumulation issue. Error banners do not auto-deduplicate. Both methods append to the message area without removing previous entries. The solution requires explicit clearing, not switching message types. The `g_form` message API treats info and error messages identically in terms of accumulation behavior; both stack on repeated calls, and both are removed by `g_form.clearMessages()` when proper cleanup is implemented.
Moving the logic to an onSubmit Client Script does not address the accumulation problem during field changes. onSubmit scripts execute during form submission, not during repeated field change events. If the goal is to provide feedback as users fill out the form, the messages must be managed in onChange scripts with proper clearing logic. Additionally, onSubmit is typically used for final validation before the record is saved, not for providing real-time guidance during form completion, which is the purpose of onChange client scripts.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug client-side scripts for desktop

questions.question:
A Developer uses `jslog()` in a client script and expects output in the browser developer console, but nothing appears there.
What explains this?
options: `jslog()` works in server-side Script Includes and requires GlideSystem context
`jslog()` output is suppressed unless ACL debug mode is enabled globally
`jslog()` writes to ServiceNow's JavaScript Log tooling
`jslog()` writes when the page is opened through Service Portal widgets
questions.explanation:
`jslog()` writes to ServiceNow's JavaScript Log tooling, not to the browser's built-in developer console. The JavaScript Log is a platform-specific debugging tool that captures client-side log output separately from the browser's built-in console. Developers must enable the JavaScript Log and Field Watcher debug listener to view jslog output. For browser console output, `console.log()` is used instead. The JavaScript Log is activated through the debug menu and provides a dedicated output window within the platform's classic UI interface for reviewing client-side diagnostic messages.
`jslog()` does not work in server-side Script Includes and does not require GlideSystem context. `jslog()` is a client-side debugging function available in browser-executed scripts such as Client Scripts and UI Policies.
