Server-side logging uses `gs.log()`, `gs.info()`, and related GlideSystem methods. `jslog()` has no GlideSystem context because it operates entirely in the browser environment. Attempting to call `jslog()` in a server-side Script Include would produce an undefined function error because the function is only defined in the client-side JavaScript runtime loaded by the platform UI.
`jslog()` does not write when the page is opened through Service Portal widgets. Service Portal uses a different rendering framework, and `jslog()` is a function available in the classic platform UI's client-side scripting environment. Portal widget scripts use Angular-based patterns and do not have access to the classic platform's `jslog()` function. Portal widgets have their own debugging mechanisms, and developers working in the Service Portal context typically use `console.log()` or Angular debugging tools rather than platform-specific functions tied to the classic form rendering engine.
`jslog()` output is not suppressed unless ACL debug mode is enabled globally. `jslog()` output routing is controlled by the JavaScript Log and Field Watcher debugging tools, not by ACL debug configuration. ACL debugging is a separate feature that traces security rule evaluation and has no relationship to client-side JavaScript log output. ACL debug mode writes security evaluation traces to the server-side system log, showing which ACL rules were evaluated and whether access was granted or denied.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug client-side scripts for desktop

questions.question: How does a Developer obtain fast root-cause isolation across message output and execution flow while debugging desktop client scripts?
options: Using Scheduled Script Execution logs as the primary debugger for onChange handlers
Using update-set preview conflict logs to debug browser runtime exceptions
Using browser developer tools breakpoints and network inspection
Using transform map preview output to trace client-side form events
Using `jslog()` /platform JavaScript log tools to trace execution
questions.explanation:
Using `jslog()` and platform JavaScript log tools to trace execution is appropriate for client-side debugging. These tools capture execution flow and variable values within the ServiceNow client-side scripting environment. The JavaScript Log and Field Watcher provide platform-specific visibility into how Client Scripts, UI Policies, and other client-side components execute during form interactions. Developers can insert `jslog()` statements at key decision points in their scripts to trace which code paths are taken and what values variables hold at each stage of execution.
Using browser developer tools breakpoints and network inspection is appropriate. These are standard client-side debugging techniques that work directly with the JavaScript running in the browser. Breakpoints pause execution at specific lines, and network inspection reveals Asynchronous JavaScript and XML (AJAX) calls and server responses. Together they provide comprehensive visibility into client-side behavior and server communication. The Sources panel allows stepping through Client Script code line by line, while the Network panel shows GlideAjax request payloads and response data, helping isolate whether issues originate client-side or server-side. Using Scheduled Script Execution logs as the primary debugger for onChange handlers is not appropriate. Scheduled scripts run on timed schedules on the server side and have no connection to client-side form events. onChange handlers execute in the browser when field values change, and their debugging requires client-side tools, not server-side scheduled job output. Scheduled Script Execution is designed for automated background tasks such as data maintenance, report generation, and periodic cleanup operations that run without user interaction.
Using transform map preview output to trace client-side form events is not appropriate. Transform maps process data during import operations, mapping source fields to target table columns. Transform map previews show how source data maps to target fields during data import and are used to verify import configurations before committing records. They operate entirely within the data import pipeline and have no connection to the client-side form scripting environment.
Using update-set preview conflict logs to debug browser runtime exceptions is not appropriate. Update-set previews identify configuration conflicts when applying update sets to target instances. They operate at the migration and deployment level, not at the runtime script execution level. Browser exceptions require browser developer tools or platform client-side debugging features. Update-set conflicts arise when the same configuration artifact exists in both the source and target instance with different values, which is a deployment concern unrelated to diagnosing JavaScript errors during live form interactions.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug client-side scripts for desktop

questions.question: Which APIs are recommended for client-side use?
options: `GlideRecord`
`g_form`
`g_user`
questions.explanation:
`g_form` is recommended for client-side use. It is the primary API for interacting with form elements in the browser. It provides methods for getting and setting field values, controlling visibility and mandatory status, and displaying messages. `g_form` is automatically available in Client Scripts and UI Policies that execute during form rendering. Common methods include `getValue()`, `setValue()`, `setMandatory()`, `setVisible()`, `setReadOnly()`, `addInfoMessage()`, and `getReference()`, all of which manipulate the form interface in real time.
`g_user` is recommended for client-side use. It provides information about the currently logged-in user within browser-executed scripts. It exposes methods for checking user roles, retrieving the user's name and sys_id, and accessing client-side user session data. `g_user` is available in Client Scripts and UI Policies. Key methods include `g_user.hasRole()` for role checking, `g_user.getFullName()` for the display name, and `g_user.userID` for the current user's sys_id, enabling scripts to customize form behavior based on who is viewing the record.
`GlideRecord` is not recommended for client-side use. It is a server-side API for database operations. While a limited synchronous GlideRecord exists in some client environments for backward compatibility, it blocks the browser thread and is not recommended. The supported pattern for client scripts requiring server data is GlideAjax calling a Script Include. Client-side GlideRecord usage generates performance warnings and can freeze the browser during execution, making it unsuitable for production code where responsive user experience is required.
`gs` (GlideSystem) is not recommended for client-side use. It is a server-side API providing system-level methods such as `getUserID()`, `log()`, and `addInfoMessage()`. Calling `gs` methods in a Client Script produces a "gs is not defined" error. The client-side equivalent for user information is the `g_user` object. Server-side `gs` methods are available in Business Rules, Script Includes, scheduled scripts, and other server-side execution contexts. Developers must use client-side alternatives like `g_user` and `g_form` for equivalent functionality in browser scripts.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug client-side scripts for desktop

questions.question: Which GlideRecord pattern is preferred for a server script that already has a specific `sys_id` and needs to look up one record?
options: `addQuery('sys_id', id)`
`addQuery()` with `setLimit(1)` and `next()`
`gr.get(sys_id)`
`gr.get()` with a display value string
questions.explanation:
Using `gr.get(sys_id)` is preferred because it retrieves a single record by its primary key in one optimized method call. The `get()` method is optimized for single-record lookups by sys_id, combining the query construction and execution into a single operation. It is more concise and efficient than the multi-step addQuery/query/next pattern when the sys_id is already known. The method returns true if a record is found and false otherwise, allowing immediate conditional checks without additional iteration logic.
Using `addQuery('sys_id', id)` followed by `query()` and `next()` is not the preferred pattern. This pattern is appropriate for complex queries with multiple conditions, but for a simple single-record lookup by sys_id, `gr.get()` is the preferred shorthand that communicates intent more clearly and reduces code volume. The addQuery/query/next pattern is designed for building filtered queries that may return multiple records.
Using `addQuery()` with `setLimit(1)` and iterating with `next()` is unnecessarily complex for a single-record lookup when the sys_id is known. While `setLimit(1)` prevents processing multiple records, the pattern still requires addQuery, query, and next calls. The setLimit method is valuable for performance optimization when querying tables with potentially large result sets, but it adds no benefit over `get()` for primary key lookups.
Using `gr.get()` with a display value string instead of a `sys_id` fails to retrieve the record. The `get()` method expects a sys_id value as its parameter, not a display value. Passing a display value string will not match any record because the method searches the sys_id column specifically. For lookups by display value, the developer must use `addQuery()` with the appropriate field name and display value string, then call `query()` and `next()` to iterate the results.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug server-side scripts

questions.question:
A scheduled script sets a date-time value near midnight UTC. Users in negative time zones see the date as the previous day on forms.
What causes this to happen?
options: The Date/Time field's dictionary type defaults to Date-only.
UTC conversion occurs in client scripts.
GlideDateTime values are UTC-based.
GlideDateTime stores values per user locale.
questions.explanation:
GlideDateTime values are UTC-based. When a value is set near midnight UTC, users in time zones with negative UTC offsets see the adjusted local time, which can fall on the previous calendar day. This is expected behavior; the platform converts UTC to the user's configured time zone at display time.
GlideDateTime does not store values per user locale. All date-time values are stored as a single UTC value in the database regardless of which user created or modified the record. The platform performs time zone conversion at display time based on each user's configured time zone preference. This centralized UTC storage ensures consistency across users in different locations. If the platform stored per-locale values, two users viewing the same record would see the same timestamp, and scheduled jobs or Business Rules would lack a reliable canonical time reference for calculations.
UTC conversion does not occur in client scripts. The platform handles UTC-to-local conversion at the server level during form rendering, and again in list views and reports. Client scripts receive already-converted display values through g_form. The date shift in this scenario results from server-side UTC offset calculation, not from client-side script processing. When developers need to work with date-time values in server-side scripts, they should use GlideDateTime methods that account for time zone differences rather than performing manual string-based time calculations.
The Date/Time field's dictionary type does not default to Date-only. Date and Date/Time are distinct field types in the dictionary. If a Date/Time field shows unexpected dates, it is due to time zone conversion of the stored UTC value, not because the field type discards time information. The Date type stores only a calendar date without time, while Date/Time stores both date and time in UTC format. These are separate dictionary types selected during field creation and cannot change their behavior at runtime.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug server-side scripts

questions.question:
A Script Include is marked `Client callable`. A Developer tries to instantiate it directly in browser code as if it were local JavaScript. It fails.
What explains this?
options: `Client callable` allows invocation through GlideAjax.
`Client callable` bypasses ACL and cross-scope checks.
`Client callable` copies the Script Include into the page DOM.
`Client callable` allows direct calls when the Script Include is in Global scope.
questions.explanation:
`Client callable` allows invocation through GlideAjax, not direct instantiation in browser code. Developers must use GlideAjax to construct the request, specify parameters, and handle the asynchronous response. The `Client callable` checkbox exposes the Script Include as an Asynchronous JavaScript and XML (AJAX) endpoint that GlideAjax can target, but it does not change the execution environment. The Script Include's code runs on the server with full access to server-side APIs like GlideRecord and GlideSystem.
`Client callable` does not copy the Script Include into the page Document Object Model (DOM). The Script Include remains a server-side artifact at all times. Marking it as client callable creates an endpoint that GlideAjax can target, but the script's code never transfers to or executes in the browser. Direct instantiation in JavaScript fails because the class definition does not exist in the browser's runtime environment. Server-side Script Includes are stored in the sys_script_include table and executed by the server-side JavaScript engine, keeping their logic isolated from browser-accessible code.
`Client callable` does not allow direct calls when the Script Include is in Global scope. Scope has no effect on whether a Script Include can be directly instantiated in client-side JavaScript. Regardless of scope, Script Includes execute on the server. `Client callable` enables GlideAjax-based invocation, not direct browser-side instantiation, in any scope. Application scope governs which server-side resources can access each other through cross-scope access policies, but it does not change the fundamental client-server boundary that separates browser JavaScript from server-side Script Include execution.
`Client callable` does not bypass ACL and cross-scope checks. Marking a Script Include as client callable exposes it to GlideAjax requests but does not alter the security or cross-scope governance model. ACL evaluations and scope access rules still apply when the Script Include executes on the server in response to a GlideAjax call. This is an important security consideration because client-callable Script Includes are accessible from any browser session. Developers should validate input parameters and enforce appropriate access controls within the Script Include to prevent unauthorized data access.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug server-side scripts

questions.question:
A Developer adds gs.debug() statements to a Script Include in a scoped application to trace execution during testing. The gs.debug() statements produce no output in the System Log, while gs.error() statements in the same Script Include do.
What explains this?
options: The gs.debug() method writes to the browser console instead of the System Log.
The gs.debug() method is available only in Script Includes in the global scope.
The gs.debug() method is suppressed when it runs inside try-catch blocks.
The application logging verbosity is set to a level above debug.
questions.explanation:
In a scoped application, the logging verbosity property of the application, <scope>.logging.verbosity, determines which logging methods write to the System Log. When it is set to a level above debug, such as info or error, gs.debug() statements are discarded while gs.error() statements are still written. The Developer sets the property to debug during testing.
The gs.debug() method is a server-side GlideSystem method and writes to the System Log. Browser console output comes from client-side code.
The gs.debug() method is available in scoped server-side scripts, including scoped Script Includes. The gs.error() output in the same Script Include also shows that logging works in this scope.
A try-catch block affects how errors propagate. It does not change whether logging methods write output.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug server-side scripts

questions.question: Which approaches do Developers use for server-side debugging and validation?
options: Use browser network panel timing as the source of server Business Rule diagnostics
Use `g_form` console traces as primary evidence of Business Rule execution order
Add targeted logging with `gs.info()/gs.warn()/gs.error()` around decision branches
Use Script Debugger/transaction-level debugging to inspect server script execution context
questions.explanation:
Adding targeted logging with `gs.info()`, `gs.warn()`, or `gs.error()` around decision branches is a valid server-side debugging approach because these methods write consistently to the system log with defined severity levels. They provide reliable diagnostic output that can be reviewed in the System Log module to trace execution flow, variable values, and decision points within Business Rules and other server-side scripts. Using structured log messages with contextual information such as record sys_id, field values, and script identifiers makes it easier to filter and correlate log entries during troubleshooting.
Using Script Debugger and transaction-level debugging to inspect server script execution context is a valid approach because the Script Debugger allows developers to set breakpoints, step through server-side code, and examine variables in real time. Transaction-level debugging captures the full execution sequence including Business Rules, allowing developers to understand script behavior and identify issues in their server-side logic. The debugger provides a controlled environment for inspecting the state of GlideRecord objects, variable values, and execution paths at each step of a Business Rule's processing cycle.
Using `g_form` console traces as primary evidence of Business Rule execution order is not valid for server-side debugging. `g_form` is a client-side API that operates in the browser and has no visibility into server-side Business Rule execution. Business Rules run on the server, and their diagnostics must come from server-side logging, debugger tools, or database audit trails. Business Rules execute in a defined order based on their type (before, after, async, display) and configured order field values, but this execution sequence is only observable through server-side diagnostic tools.
Using browser network panel timing as the source of server Business Rule diagnostics is not appropriate. Server-side debugging requires server-side tools like logging, Script Debugger, or transaction logs that capture the actual execution context. The network panel shows HTTP request and response metadata such as status codes, headers, and payload sizes, but it treats the server-side processing as an opaque operation with no visibility into individual script executions.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug server-side scripts

questions.question:
A Record Producer targets the Facilities Request table, which has a Requested for [requested_for] field. The Record Producer collects the requester in a variable named requester and has no script. Users fill in the variable, but the Requested for field is empty on the created records.
What explains this?
options: Variables map to fields only when their labels match the field labels.
Variables map to fields only after a flow processes the new record.
The variable has no mapping to the Requested for field.
Record Producer variable answers are stored only on a Requested Item.
questions.explanation:
A Record Producer copies a variable's value to a field of the target table when the variable name matches the field name, or when Map to field is selected and the field is chosen. The variable name requester differs from requested_for, Map to field is not configured, and no script assigns the value. The Developer selects Map to field and chooses Requested for, or sets current.requested_for = producer.requester in the script.
A Record Producer creates a record on its target table. It does not create a Requested Item, so its answers are not stored only on a Requested Item.
Mapping uses the variable name or the Map to field setting. Labels are display text and play no part in mapping.
Variable values are mapped when the Record Producer creates the record. No flow is required for the mapping.
questions.reference: Use a Record Producer as an application's UI

questions.question:
A Record Producer script sets `current.short_description = current.requested_for;` and the produced record's short description is blank. The requester filled the variable on the form.
What explains this behavior?
options: Record Producer variables are readable only in catalog client scripts.
Variable values are available only after the record is committed.
The `current` object is unavailable in Record Producer scripts.
Variable answers are accessed through `producer.<variable_name>`.
questions.explanation:
Variable answers are accessed through `producer.<variable_name>`, not through `current`. The `current` object represents the target record being created, which does not have variables; it has table fields. To read a variable named `requested_for` and copy it to `current.requested_for`, the script must use `producer.requested_for`, not `current.requested_for`.
`current` is not unavailable in Record Producer scripts. The `current` object is available and represents the target table record being created. Variables live on the `producer` object, fields live on the `current` object. The `current object in this context behaves like a standard GlideRecord for the target table, and the Developer can set field values on it using `current.field_name = value` before the record is inserted.
Record Producer variables are not readable only in catalog client scripts. Variables are accessible in Record Producer server scripts through the `producer object. Catalog client scripts run in the browser and use different patterns, but server-side Record Producer scripts can read all variable values via `producer.<variable_name>` and write them to the target record. The `producer` object provides access to all submitted variable answers, allowing the server-side script to validate, transform, and assign values to the target record before the insert operation completes.
Variable values are not available only after the record is committed. Variable values are accessible throughout the Record Producer script execution, including before the insert occurs. The `producer` object contains all submitted variable answers at the time the script runs, allowing the Developer to read, validate, and map values before or during record creation. The Record Producer script executes before the target record is inserted, giving the developer an opportunity to set field values on `current`, perform validation against submitted variables, and abort the operation if business rules are not satisfied.
questions.reference: Use a Record Producer as an application's UI

questions.question:
A Record Producer script calls current.setAbortAction (true) when the submitted values fail validation. Users see a blank page after they submit.
What does the Developer add to the script so that users see a meaningful page?
options: Set producer.redirect to the URL of a page that explains the error
Call current.update() before the call to current.setAbortAction(true)
Add a Catalog UI Policy that shows a message when validation fails
Move the validation to a Scheduled Script Execution that runs after submission
questions.explanation:
In a Record Producer script, producer.redirect is a property that defines the page users see after submission, for example producer.redirect = 'catalog_home.do';. Combined with gs.addErrorMessage(), it takes users to a page that explains why the record was not created instead of a blank page.
Calling current.update() saves the record before the abort, which defeats the validation. It does not provide feedback to the user.
A Catalog UI Policy runs in the browser before submission and is configured outside the script. It cannot respond to an abort that the server-side script performs after submission.
A Scheduled Script Execution runs on a schedule in the background, unrelated to the user's submission. It cannot redirect the user or display a message.
questions.reference: Use a Record Producer as an application's UI

questions.question:
A team configures a new Record Producer with the minimum settings needed to collect data from users and create records.
Which two configuration areas does the team use?
options: Catalog client script configuration
Variable configuration
Access control and role restrictions
Category and catalog assignment
Target table configuration
questions.explanation:
The target table defines where the Record Producer creates a record when a user submits it. A Record Producer creates a record on its target table, such as Incident or a custom application table; it does not create Request or Requested Item records.
Variables define the data that users enter on the Record Producer. Without variables, the form collects no information, and variable values are copied to target table fields through matching names, Map to field, or the Record Producer script.
Catalog client scripts add dynamic behavior, such as showing variables or validating input before submission. They are optional for a working Record Producer.
Restrictions on who can see or submit the Record Producer are governance settings. They are recommended for production use, but the Record Producer collects data and creates records without them.
Categories and catalogs determine where users find the Record Producer in the catalog. They improve discoverability but are not required for submission and record creation.
questions.reference: Use a Record Producer as an application's UI

questions.question: Why does a Developer with only the `x_acme_ops.admin` role have access to user-level functionality in an app?
options: Module visibility rules promote user-role privileges into the admin role at runtime.
Any `.admin` suffix role grants user-level privileges through a global inheritance handoff.
ACL evaluation treats app admin as equivalent to `security_admin` for many app tables.
The admin role contains the user role through role inheritance, granting user-level permissions automatically.
questions.explanation:
The Developer already has user-level access because ServiceNow role inheritance allows one role to contain another, so the containing role automatically inherits all permissions from the contained role. When an App Owner configures the admin role to contain the user role, assigning admin to a user grants both admin-level and user-level permissions. This eliminates the need to assign both roles separately and follows the principle that higher-privilege roles should include lower-privilege access.
A naming convention handoff is not why the Developer has user-level privileges. ServiceNow does not automatically grant user-level privileges to any role ending in `.admin`. Role inheritance must be explicitly configured through the Contains Roles related list on the role record itself. The `.admin` and `.user` suffixes are naming conventions that help developers organize roles logically, but they carry no automatic functional meaning to the platform's role evaluation engine and do not trigger implicit handoff.
Module visibility rules do not explain why the developer has user-level access. These rules control navigator display, not role privilege inheritance between roles. Module visibility is evaluated at navigation render time and is entirely separate from the role inheritance system. Role inheritance is configured statically in the role hierarchy through the Contains Roles related list and affects all permissions system-wide, not just module visibility.
Access Control List (ACL) equivalence with `security_admin` does not explain why the developer has user-level access. Application-scoped admin roles like `x_acme_ops.admin` are not treated as equivalent to the global `security_admin role`. The `security_admin` role has elevated platform-wide privileges specifically for security configuration tasks, while scoped app admin roles are limited to their application scope. ACL evaluation respects the specific roles listed in each ACL rule and does not automatically substitute or elevate scoped admin roles to global admin status.
questions.reference: Restrict access to applications and application modules

questions.question:
A module has `Override application menu roles` enabled and its own role set to `itil`. The parent Application Menu requires `admin`. A user has `itil` but not `admin`.
What is the expected visibility outcome?
options: The user sees the module only if an ACL also grants navigator access for `itil`.
The user sees the module because the override bypasses the parent menu role check.
The user cannot see the module because menu roles are evaluated after module roles.
The user cannot see the module because override requires both menu and module roles to match.
questions.explanation:
The user sees the module because the `Override application menu roles` checkbox allows a module to bypass the parent Application Menu's role requirements and evaluate visibility based solely on the module's own role field. When enabled, the user only needs to possess the module role (itil) regardless of whether they have the parent menu role (admin). This feature is essential for creating targeted navigation paths where specific modules need different access control than their parent menu structure.
The user can see the module, not be blocked from it, because the override setting bypasses the parent menu's admin requirement. By default ServiceNow checks the parent Application Menu role first and then the module's own role, so this choice actually reverses the real evaluation order. With `Override application menu roles` enabled, the parent check is skipped altogether; the admin requirement never comes into play, and the user's itil role alone is enough to grant visibility.
An access control list (ACL) is not required for the user to see the module. ACLS control access to table operations like read, write, create, and delete on records, but they do not govern whether navigation modules appear in the application navigator. Navigator visibility is a separate authorization layer that operates independently from the ACL framework and is managed through the sys_app_module table configuration.
The purpose of the override setting is the opposite: it allows the module to be visible when the module role is satisfied even if the parent menu role is not satisfied. If override required both roles to match, it would provide no functional benefit. The override setting exists specifically to create exceptions where certain modules within an application menu should be accessible to users who lack the broader menu role but have specific module-level access.
questions.reference: Restrict access to applications and application modules

questions.question: An application must be available to 400 users, and the user population changes every month. Which role assignment approach provides access with the least maintenance?
options: Create an ACL for each module that checks group membership
Import the users through LDAP and map roles in a transform map
Assign the application roles to each user on the User form
Assign the application roles to groups and manage group membership
questions.explanation:
Assigning roles to groups lets administrators grant or remove access by changing group membership. Users inherit the roles of the groups they belong to, so a monthly change in the user population requires no role changes, and access can be audited by reviewing group membership.
Assigning roles to individual users requires a change to each user record whenever the population changes. With 400 users and monthly changes, this approach creates the most maintenance.
Access control lists (ACLs) protect records and fields. They do not control whether modules appear in the application navigator, and an ACL per module adds configuration without granting the application roles.
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) imports can create or update user records, but a transform map is a data-load mechanism, not the ongoing way to manage role assignment.
questions.reference: Restrict access to applications and application modules

questions.question:
A Developer creates a table in a scoped application and creates no access control lists explicitly. Users without the application's roles are unable to read the table's records.
What explains this?
options: Table creation generated default ACLs that require the table's user role.
Menu role restrictions generate table ACLs for every application module.
Dictionary defaults on scoped tables block read access until security_admin is elevated.
Scoped tables inherit global ACLs that deny access to users without the admin role.
questions.explanation:
When a table is created with Create access controls selected, which is the default, the platform generates create, read, write, and delete access control lists (ACLs) for the table. All four ACLS require the role selected in the table's User role field. Users without that role are denied, even though the Developer created no ACLs manually.
ACLs are matched to the table they protect. The new table has its own generated ACLs; it does not inherit a global rule that denies non-admin users.
Application menu and module roles control what appears in the application navigator. They do not generate ACLs.
Dictionary entries define fields and their attributes. They do not control read access, and elevating to security_admin is required only to modify ACLs.
questions.reference: Restrict access to applications and application modules

questions.question:
A custom role hierarchy is defined where `x_app.supervisor` contains `x_app.agent`. An admin removes `x_app.agent` from a user but keeps `x_app.supervisor`.
What happens?
options: The user loses agent-level permissions because removing the role breaks the containment chain.
The user loses agent-level permissions because containment does not apply in scoped apps.
The user still retains agent-level permissions through the containing supervisor role.
The user retains module access but loses ACL-protected table operations.
questions.explanation:
The user still retains agent-level permissions because in ServiceNow role inheritance, the containing role (supervisor) inherits all permissions from the contained role (agent). This reduces administrative complexity. When a role contains another role, it means the containing role includes all the privileges of the contained role automatically. Therefore, a user with only the supervisor role still has agent-level permissions because supervisor was configured to contain agent.
The user does not lose agent-level permissions because removing the directly assigned agent role does not break the containment chain. In ServiceNow, the containing role inherits permissions from the contained role, not the other way around. When supervisor contains agent, supervisor gets agent permissions. Removing the agent role from a user who still has supervisor does not remove agent-level access because supervisor already includes those permissions through the containment relationship.
The user does not retain only module access while losing access control list (ACL)-protected table operations. Role containment affects all authorization checks throughout the platform, including ACL evaluation, module visibility, and scripted security checks. When an ACL requires a specific role, users with containing roles also satisfy that requirement. The role inheritance system is a core security feature that operates consistently across all role-based authorization mechanisms in ServiceNow.
The user does not lose agent-level permissions because containment works identically in both Global scope and scoped applications. The role inheritance mechanism is a platform-level feature that operates uniformly regardless of application scope. Scoped applications can define their own roles and configure role containment relationships that function the same way as global roles. Scope affects artifact visibility and access, but it does not change how role containment operates within its security model.
questions.reference: Restrict access to applications and application modules

questions.question: What ensures module visibility in a scoped app?
options: Table field ACL for `*` is set to read for authenticated users.
User has required role(s) on the module.
Module link type and arguments resolve to a valid target table.
Parent Application Menu role checks are satisfied.
questions.explanation:
Having the required role(s) on the module is a mandatory visibility condition. Users must possess at least one of the listed roles for the module to appear in the navigator. This fundamental visibility check occurs when the navigator is rendered. Without the required module roles, the module remains hidden regardless of other conditions. Role-based module visibility ensures that users only see navigation options appropriate to their authorization level.
Satisfying parent Application Menu role checks is a required visibility condition. Application Menus can have their own role requirements. Unless the module has `Override application menu roles` enabled, the user must satisfy both the Application Menu role requirements and the module role requirements for the module to be visible. Parent menu role checks act as a first-tier filter for entire sections of the navigator, ensuring users only see application areas they are authorized to access.
Table field access control lists (ACLS) control access to data operations on records, not module visibility in the navigator. Module visibility is determined by role checks on the module and parent menu records, not by ACLs. While ACLs will affect whether users can successfully perform operations after navigating to a module, they do not determine whether the module appears in the navigator.
Module link type and argument validity is not a required visibility condition. Users would still see the module but might encounter errors when attempting to use it if the link is misconfigured. Module visibility is controlled by role checks and active status, not by the validity of link targets.
questions.reference: Restrict access to applications and application modules

questions.question:
A Developer adds a script to an ACL to block unauthorized users. Testing shows that the script is skipped for certain users, who are denied before the script runs.
Which ACL evaluation behavior explains this?
options: The ACL skips the role check when both a condition and a script are configured.
The ACL checks the condition first to reduce the cost of the role check.
The ACL checks roles first, and a failed role check skips the condition and script.
The ACL runs the script first and checks roles only when the script returns true.
questions.explanation:
An access control list (ACL) evaluates its requirements in order: required roles, then the condition, then the script. If the user lacks the required roles, the ACL denies access and the condition and script are not evaluated. Users who fail the role check never reach the script.
Scripts are evaluated last because they are the most expensive part of the rule. Checking roles first avoids running scripts for users who lack the required roles.
The condition is evaluated after the role check. The condition is a filter on record fields defined with the condition builder; JavaScript logic belongs in the script.
The role check is always evaluated when roles are defined. All configured parts of the ACL must evaluate to true for the ACL to grant access.
questions.reference: Manually and automatically create, test, and debug Access Controls

questions.question:
A table ACL grants users read access to records. One sensitive field should remain hidden from those users.
What does a Developer do?
options: Extend the table ACL to cover individual field access
Add a field-level ACL for the sensitive field
Rely on the table ACL to mask the field automatically
Configure a UI Policy to hide the field
questions.explanation:
The Developer adds a field-level ACL for the sensitive field. Even when users have read access to a table through a table access control list (ACL), specific fields can be protected using field-level ACLs that require additional roles or conditions. Field ACLs follow the pattern `table_name.field_name` and allow administrators to enforce tighter security on sensitive data like salary, SSN, or confidential notes within otherwise accessible records.
The Developer does not rely on the table ACL to mask the field automatically. A table ACL grants or denies access to the entire table or specific operations on records but does not distinguish between fields within those records. If a user has read access through a table ACL, they can see all fields unless specific field ACLs are created to restrict individual field visibility.
The Developer does not configure a UI Policy to hide the field. UI Policies are client-side controls that can be bypassed through APIs, web services, or direct database access. For security that enforces field protection regardless of access method, field ACLs must be used. UI Policies improve user experience but should not be relied upon for access control.
The Developer does not extend the table ACL to cover individual field access. A read ACL controls whether users can view records, while field-level ACLS control access to specific fields within those records. ServiceNow evaluates ACLs based on the specific operation and the specific object being accessed, and table ACLs do not inherit downward to individual fields.
questions.reference: Manually and automatically create, test, and debug Access Controls

questions.question:
A field-level read ACL on x_acme_hr_case.salary requires the x_acme_hr.manager role. During testing, a Developer who has only the admin role can still read the field.
What explains this?
options: Field-level ACLs are evaluated only during impersonation.
Field-level ACLs apply only to list views.
The ACL has Admin overrides selected.
The table-level read ACL overrides the field-level ACL.
questions.explanation:
When Admin overrides is selected on an access control list (ACL), users with the admin role pass the ACL even if they do not meet its other requirements. To test the restriction, the Developer impersonates a user who lacks the x_acme_hr.manager role or clears Admin overrides on the ACL.
Field-level ACLs apply wherever the field is accessed, including forms, lists, and exports. They are not limited to list views.
A user must pass the table-level ACL and then the field-level ACL to read a field. The table-level ACL does not override the field-level ACL.
ACLs are evaluated for every session. Impersonation only changes which user the ACLs evaluate.
questions.reference: Manually and automatically create, test, and debug Access Controls

questions.question:
A table has a wildcard ACL `x_app_case.*` and a specific ACL `x_app_case.priority`. Access to `priority` differs from other fields.
What causes this to happen?
options: The specific field ACL takes precedence over the wildcard ACL.
Wildcard field ACL overrides specific field ACLs to enforce consistency.
Specific field ACLS apply when table ACLs are inactive.
Wildcard ACL applies to list views, while specific ACL applies to form views.
questions.explanation:
The specific field access control list (ACL) takes precedence over the wildcard ACL. Access to the priority field differs from other fields because ServiceNow ACL evaluation follows a specificity hierarchy: more specific ACL rules take precedence over more general ones. A field ACL targeting `x_app_case.priority` is more specific than a wildcard field ACL `x_app_case.*`, so the specific field ACL governs access to the priority field while the wildcard ACL governs all other fields.
Wildcard field ACL does not override specific field ACLs. The ACL framework gives precedence to the most specific matching rule, meaning a field-specific ACL will govern that field's access even when a wildcard ACL exists. If wildcard ACLs overrode specific ones, it would be impossible to create field-level exceptions within a table, defeating the purpose of having both wildcard and specific field ACL capabilities.
Specific field ACLs do not apply only when table ACLs are inactive. Field ACLS and table ACLs serve different purposes and operate independently. Table ACLS control access to records or table operations, while field ACLS control access to individual fields within records. Both types of ACLs are evaluated based on the operation being performed, and field ACL evaluation is not conditional on table ACL status.
Wildcard ACL does not apply only to list views, and specific ACL does not apply only to form views. Both wildcard and specific field ACLs are evaluated consistently across UI contexts. The distinction between specific and wildcard ACLs is based on specificity precedence, not on which UI view is being accessed. ACLs apply uniformly regardless of whether data is viewed in a list or form.
questions.reference: Manually and automatically create, test, and debug Access Controls

questions.question: Which ACL operation is missing when users can perform updates, but inserts fail?
options: `execute`
`read`
`create`
`write`
questions.explanation:
The missing operation is `create`. The write operation controls whether users can update existing records by modifying field values, while the create operation controls whether users can insert new records into the table. ServiceNow separates these operations to allow granular control. Users need explicit create access control list (ACL) authorization to insert new records.
Write is not the missing operation. The scenario states that users already have write ACL permission and can successfully update existing records. The write operation specifically governs modifications to existing records, not the insertion of new ones.
Read is not the missing operation. Read controls whether users can view records and does not govern the ability to insert new records. Read is typically the most permissive operation, allowing users to retrieve and display data. The scenario describes users who can update existing records (write access) but cannot create new ones, indicating that read access is already granted.
Execute is not the missing operation. Execute is not a standard table-level ACL operation for tables in ServiceNow. Execute operations apply to specific contexts like Script Includes, Processors, or other executable artifacts, not to standard table data operations. The primary ACL operations for tables are read, write, create, delete, and the wildcard (*) that covers all operations.
questions.reference: Manually and automatically create, test, and debug Access Controls

questions.question: What is appropriate for ACL debugging?
options: Reordering application modules to force ACL precedence resolution
Regenerating update sets so ACL checks run in deployment order
Validating operation/object specificity for the target action
Testing role, condition, and script branches independently
questions.explanation:
Validating operation and object specificity is an appropriate debugging action. ACL issues often stem from mismatches between the intended and actual operation or object. ACLs match based on the combination of operation (read, write, create, delete) and object (table name, field name), and specificity matters. Verifying these settings ensures the intended rule is being evaluated. For example, a write ACL does not affect read operations, and a table ACL does not protect specific fields without corresponding field ACLs.
Testing role, condition, and script branches independently is an appropriate debugging action. ACLs evaluate these three components in sequence. Isolating each component helps determine whether the unexpected behavior stems from role assignment, conditional logic, or script code. Developers can verify role membership first, then test condition expressions, and finally review script execution to pinpoint the failure point. This methodical approach accelerates ACL troubleshooting and ensures each evaluation component behaves as intended.
Application module order does not affect ACL precedence or evaluation in any way. Modules control navigator visibility and organization, while ACLS control data access authorization. These are entirely separate systems with no interaction regarding precedence or evaluation order. ACL matching is based on operation and object specificity, not module ordering. Reordering modules would have no impact on ACL evaluation behavior and would not help diagnose or debug ACL issues.
Update set deployment order does not affect ACL evaluation at runtime. Once ACL records are deployed and exist in the system, they are evaluated based on operation/object matching and specificity rules, not based on when or in what order they were deployed. Regenerating update sets is an administrative task related to deployment and version control, not a troubleshooting technique for ACL behavior. ACL evaluation is determined by configuration content, not deployment sequence.
questions.reference: Manually and automatically create, test, and debug Access Controls

questions.question:
A script checks `gs.hasRole('x_app.approver')` and returns `true`, but no administrator granted that role to the user individually.
What explains this?
options: `gs.hasRole()` returns true for roles listed on ACL rules.
`gs.hasRole()` evaluates roles only when called in ACL script context.
`gs.hasRole()` checks direct user-role records.
`gs.hasRole()` evaluates effective roles.
questions.explanation:
`gs.hasRole()` evaluates effective roles. In this scenario, the user has the role through group membership or role containment because `gs.hasRole()` evaluates a user's effective roles, not just direct assignments. Roles obtained this way still appear in the user's Roles related list as inherited roles. The method also returns true for any user with the admin role. The method does not distinguish between assignment sources; it simply checks whether the user currently has the specified role through any mechanism.
`gs.hasRole()` does not check only direct user-role records. The method evaluates the user's effective roles from all sources, including group-based role grants and inherited roles from role containment. If the method only checked direct assignments, it would fail to recognize roles granted through groups, which is the most common and scalable role assignment pattern.
`gs.hasRole()` does not return true for roles listed on access control list (ACL) rules. The method evaluates whether the current user possesses a specific role, not whether that role is listed on ACL rules. ACL configuration and role membership are separate concerns. A user can have roles that are not referenced in any ACL, and conversely, ACLs can list roles that a user does not have.
`gs.hasRole()` does not evaluate roles only when called in ACL script context. The method functions identically in Business Rules, Script Includes, Scheduled Jobs, and any other server-side execution context.
questions.reference: Use GlideSystem methods to script security

questions.question:
An ACL script contains the expression current.requested_for === gs.getUserID(). The expression evaluates to false even when the current user is the requester.
What explains this?
options: current.requested_for is a GlideElement object, while gs.getUserID() returns a string.
gs.getUserID() returns a GlideRecord object for the current user.
ACL scripts are unable to read the values of reference fields.
gs.getUserID() returns the sys_id of the user who started an impersonation.
questions.explanation:
The strict equality operator (===) compares both type and value. current.requested_for is a GlideElement object, while gs.getUserID() returns the sys_id as a string, so the comparison is false. Converting the element first, for example current.requested_for.toString() === gs.getUserID(), compares two strings. The loose operator (==) converts the GlideElement to its string value, which is why base-system scripts such as current.caller_id == gs.getUserID() work.
gs.getUserID() returns the sys_id of the current user as a string. GlideRecord objects are returned by queries, not by this method.
ACL scripts can read reference fields on current. The failure comes from the comparison operator, not from access to the field.
During impersonation, gs.getUserID () returns the sys_id of the impersonated user, which is the user being tested. Impersonation does not explain a failure for the actual requester.
questions.reference: Use GlideSystem methods to script security

questions.question:
A create ACL script checks `current.priority == 1` to allow inserts, but the insert fails even when priority is set correctly. Debugging shows the field value is null during ACL evaluation.
What explains this?
options: Create ACLs evaluate role lists; scripts are ignored for insert operations.
Create ACL scripts can read values when Data Policies run first.
Create ACLs run after insert, so `current` should contain final committed values.
Create ACL evaluation may occur when field values are uncommitted.
questions.explanation:
Create access control list (ACL) evaluation occurs during the insert process before the record is fully committed to the database, and field values may not be completely populated or stable at the time the ACL script executes. The timing of ACL evaluation in the creation workflow means that scripts attempting to check field values on `current` may encounter empty or default values rather than the values being submitted. This is a common pitfall when designing create ACLs, requiring Developers to use alternative authorization patterns or understand the evaluation timing.
Create ACLs are evaluated during the insert operation, not after it completes. The ACL must determine whether the user is authorized to create the record before the insert is allowed to proceed, so evaluation happens before commit. If create ACLS ran after the insert, they would be ineffective at preventing unauthorized record creation. The ACL framework operates as a gate-check during the operation, not as a post-operation validation.
Create ACL scripts are not ignored for insert operations. Like other ACL types, create ACLs support role, condition, and script components, evaluated in that order. Scripts are evaluated as part of the authorization check. However, they are evaluated at a point in the workflow where field values may not be fully populated, which is what makes field-based checks in create ACL scripts problematic.
Data Policies do not guarantee that field values will be available to create ACL scripts. Data Policies and ACL evaluation operate independently. Data Policies enforce mandatory fields and data integrity rules, but they do not control when ACLS evaluate or what values are visible to ACL scripts.
questions.reference: Use GlideSystem methods to script security

questions.question:
A server-side security script uses gs.getUser().isMemberOf('Service Desk'). After the group is renamed IT Service Desk, the script returns false for members of the group.
Which change keeps the check working if the group is renamed again?
options: Pass the group's sys_id to isMemberOf()
Store the group name in a system property and pass the property value to isMemberOf()
Pass the group's name to gs.hasRole()
Call g_user.isMemberOf() from a client script
questions.explanation:
The isMemberOf() method accepts a group name or a group sys_id. A name changes when the group is renamed, but the sys_id stays the same for the life of the record, so passing the sys_id keeps the check working after future renames.
The gs.hasRole() method checks roles, not group membership. A group name is not a role name.
A system property makes the name easier to update, but the check still depends on the group name and breaks again when the group is renamed until someone updates the property.
The g_user object in client scripts provides role checks but no group membership method, and security checks belong in server-side code.
questions.reference: Use GlideSystem methods to script security

questions.question:
A Script Include method updates records only when gs.hasRole('x_acme_fac.manager') returns true. The method works when managers start it from a form. When a Scheduled Script Execution calls the same method, the role check returns false every time.
What explains this?
options: The role check evaluates only during interactive user sessions.
The role check evaluates only roles assigned directly to the user.
The role check evaluates the user in the Run as field of the scheduled job.
The role check evaluates the user who created the scheduled job.
questions.explanation:
A scheduled job runs in the session of the user selected in its Run as field. The gs.hasRole() method evaluates the roles of that session user, so the check fails when the Run as user lacks the x_acme_fac.manager role. The Developer sets Run as to a user with the required role or moves the role check to the code that runs in user sessions.
The creator of the scheduled job has no effect on the session. The Run as field defines the user context.
The gs.hasRole() method evaluates effective roles, including roles inherited through groups and role containment.
The gs.hasRole() method runs in any server-side context, including scheduled jobs. It evaluates the user of the current session, whatever that session is.
questions.reference: Use GlideSystem methods to script security

questions.question: Which methods are appropriate to audit server-side security scripts that verify user authorization levels and team affiliations?
options: `gs.getSession().isInteractive()`
`gs.getUser().getRecord()`
`gs.hasRole()`
`gs.getUser().isMemberOf(...)`
`gs.getUserID()`
questions.explanation:
`gs.hasRole()` is the appropriate method for verifying whether the current user possesses a specific role or set of roles. This method evaluates effective roles from all sources including direct assignment, group membership, and role containment inheritance, making it the standard choice for authorization checks that determine user privilege levels. Security scripts commonly use `gs.hasRole()` to enforce role-based access control in Business Rules, access control list (ACL) scripts, and Script Includes.
`gs.getUser().isMemberOf()` is an appropriate method for verifying team affiliations because it checks whether the current user belongs to a specific group. Group membership often represents team affiliations, departments, or organizational units, and checking group membership is a common security pattern for determining whether users should have access based on their team assignment. This method complements role checks by providing group-based authorization, which is useful when access should be granted based on team membership rather than individual roles.
`gs.getUser().getRecord()` is not an appropriate method for verifying authorization levels or team affiliations. It retrieves a GlideRecord object for the current user's sys_user record rather than performing any security check. While this can be useful for reading user attributes like name, email, or department, it is not a security verification method. Security verification should use methods specifically designed for role and group membership evaluation.
`gs.getUserID()` is not an appropriate method for verifying authorization levels or team affiliations. It simply returns the sys_id string of the current user without evaluating any security context. While this is useful for comparisons (such as checking if the current user matches a record's assigned_to field), it is not a security verification method by itself. It does not check authorization levels or team affiliations; it only provides the user's unique identifier.
`gs.getSession().isInteractive()` is not an appropriate method for verifying authorization levels or team affiliations. It only determines whether the current session is interactive versus a background or scheduled job session. While this can be useful for conditional logic that behaves differently for interactive versus automated processes, it does not verify user authorization levels or team affiliations.
questions.reference: Use GlideSystem methods to script security

questions.question:
A Developer sets Accessible from to This application scope only on a Script Include and expects users with the admin role to lose access to the form features that use it. Users with the admin role keep access.
Why does this expectation fail?
options: Accessible from overrides ACL role checks for users of the Script Include.
Accessible from restricts which user roles can run the Script Include.
Accessible from hides the Script Include from the Script Includes list in other scopes.
Accessible from controls which application scopes can call the Script Include.
questions.explanation:
Accessible from determines whether scripts in other application scopes can call the Script Include. It is a scope-to-scope control. Users who work with forms in the Script Include's own scope are unaffected, whatever their roles.
Accessible from controls runtime calls from other scopes. It does not affect where the Script Include record is listed.
Accessible from and access control lists (ACLs) are separate mechanisms. Accessible from does not override or replace ACL role checks.
Accessible from has two values, All application scopes and This application scope only. Both describe scopes, not user roles.
questions.reference: Use Application Scope to protect application artifacts

questions.question:
A Script Include in Scope B is set to Accessible from: All application scopes. When Scope A's Business Rule calls it, the Script Include's attempt to modify a Global table is blocked.
What explains why the update is blocked?
options: Cross-scope privilege generation applies to specific supported operations.
Read-only protection policy overrides Accessible from at runtime.
The caller's scope controls the Global table update.
Scope B still needs cross-scope privilege to update the Global table.
questions.explanation:
Scope A can call the Script Include, but Scope B still needs cross-scope privilege to update the Global table. The `Accessible from` setting controls whether other scopes can invoke the Script Include, but it does not grant the Script Include's own scope access to resources in other scopes at runtime. Since the Script Include is defined in Scope B, its code executes as Scope B, and Scope B's update to the Global table is evaluated against a cross-scope privilege record for Scope B writing to the Global resource. Without that privilege, the update is blocked.
Cross-scope privilege generation does not explain this behavior. The platform can generate cross-scope privilege records during development, but the block in this scenario is not caused by the Script Include being unavailable to the caller. Scope A can invoke the Script Include. The blocked operation is the Global table update performed inside the Script Include, which is evaluated against Scope B's privileges, not against whether privilege generation supports the operation.
The caller's scope does not control the Global table update in this scenario. Scope A can invoke the Script Include, but the update is attempted by code defined in Scope B. The platform evaluates that table operation against Scope B's cross-scope access to the Global table, not merely against the scope that initiated the call.
Read-only protection policy does not override `Accessible from` at runtime. Protection policies control whether installed application artifacts can be viewed or modified after deployment. They are application-file protection settings, not the runtime access mechanism that determines whether a scoped script can read or write tables in another scope.
questions.reference: Use Application Scope to protect application artifacts

questions.question: What does the `Protected` protection policy enforce on distributed artifacts in the target instance?
options: Administrators can export Protected code in clear text through update sets.
Protected code visibility depends on Script Include `Accessible from`.
Protected code can be decrypted by users with `security_admin`.
The Protected policy encrypts artifact source code in the target instance.
questions.explanation:
The Protected policy encrypts artifact source code in the target instance. This makes the code permanently unreadable and non-editable. Publishers use this policy to protect intellectual property when distributing applications through the ServiceNow Store or to customer instances. Once deployed with Protected status, the code cannot be decrypted or viewed in the receiving instance by any user or elevated role.
Protected code cannot be decrypted by users with `security_admin`. There is no decryption mechanism available to users in the target instance, even with elevated privileges. The Protected policy uses strong encryption specifically designed to prevent code inspection in target instances. This permanent protection ensures that proprietary algorithms and business logic remain confidential regardless of the user's privilege level.
Administrators cannot export Protected code in clear text through update sets. The encryption is persistent and applies to all export and viewing operations. Update sets capture the encrypted artifact, not the original source code. This ensures that even backup and migration operations do not expose the protected intellectual property. The protection remains in effect for the lifetime of the artifact in the target instance.
Protected code visibility does not depend on the Script Include `Accessible from` setting because these are independent controls. `Accessible from` governs cross-scope invocation permissions, while protection policy governs code visibility and editability. An artifact can be Protected (unviewable) but accessible from all scopes, or vice versa. These two settings serve entirely different purposes and are configured independently.
questions.reference: Use Application Scope to protect application artifacts

questions.question: What does the `Allow configuration` setting do on a table?
options: Other scopes can change application namespace and scope identifiers.
Other scopes can add configuration metadata to that table.
Other scopes can bypass ACLs for many operations on the table.
Other scopes gain automatic read/write data access through APIs.
questions.explanation:
The `Allow configuration` setting permits other application scopes to extend the table by adding fields, business rules, client scripts, UI policies, and other configuration artifacts. This enables cross-scope collaboration and extension scenarios where one application builds upon another's data model. However, it also creates risk if applied too broadly, as external scopes can alter the table's structure and behavior in ways the original table owner may not anticipate or control.
Other scopes do not gain automatic read/write data access through APIs. `Allow configuration` does not grant data access permissions to other scopes. Data access is controlled separately through Application Access settings (Can read, Can create, Can update, Can delete) on the table.
Other scopes cannot bypass access control lists (ACLs) for operations on the table. `Allow configuration` does not bypass or override ACL enforcement. Other scopes can add configuration artifacts to the table, but those artifacts (and users accessing the table) remain subject to ACL evaluation. The setting controls metadata extensibility, not data authorization.
Other scopes cannot change application namespace and scope identifiers. These core application properties are protected and cannot be modified by external scopes regardless of configuration access settings. `Allow configuration` is limited to adding artifacts like fields and scripts to the table, not changing the owning application's identity or scope configuration.
questions.reference: Use Application Scope to protect application artifacts

questions.question:
A Script Include in Scope A queries a table in Scope B and gets a cross-scope security error, even though ACLs permit the user.
Which setting does the Developer enable?
options: Table Application Access `Can read` on the Scope B table
`Client callable` on the calling Script Include in Scope A
`Accessible from: All application scopes` on the Script Include in Scope A
`Client callable` enables cross-scope table reads from server-side scripts
questions.explanation:
The Developer enables table Application Access `Can read` on the Scope B table. For one scoped application to query tables in another scope, the table owner must explicitly enable this permission. The `Can read` checkbox in the table's Application Access settings grants other scopes permission to query records from that table. Even when ACLS allow the user to access the data, cross-scope queries are blocked by default unless Application Access is explicitly granted. This gives table owners control over which external scopes can interact with their data.
The Developer does not enable `Accessible from: All application scopes` on the Script Include in Scope A. This controls which scopes can invoke the Script Include, not whether Scope A can query tables in other scopes. The Script Include's accessibility setting affects inbound invocation permissions, while the scenario describes an outbound query from Scope A to a table in Scope B. The required setting is on the target table in Scope B, not on the calling Script Include in Scope A.
The Developer does not enable `Client callable` on the calling Script Include in Scope A. It determines whether a Script Include can be invoked from client-side scripts in the browser, not whether it can perform cross-scope queries server-side. Server-side Script Includes can query tables in other scopes subject to Application Access grants regardless of their client-callable status. Client callable affects client-server communication, not cross-scope server-side data access.
`Client callable` does not enable cross-scope table reads from server-side scripts. Server-side Script Includes perform cross-scope queries based on Application Access grants on the target table, independent of whether the Script Include is client-callable. Client callable controls whether client-side scripts can invoke the Script Include remotely. These are separate authorization mechanisms for different purposes, and neither replaces the Application Access `Can read` grant required on the Scope B table.
questions.reference: Use Application Scope to protect application artifacts

questions.question:
A publisher distributes an application and needs two levels of protection: one set of application files that customers can view in read-only form, and another set whose code stays hidden from customers.
Which two protection policies does the publisher select?
options: Protected
None
Open
Read-only
questions.explanation:
The Read-only protection policy lets users on the target instance view the application file but not change it. It fits files that customers may review for troubleshooting but must not modify.
The Protected protection policy hides the code of the application file on the target instance, so customers can neither view nor edit it. It fits proprietary logic.
There is no Open protection policy. The protection policy of an application file is either empty, Read-only, or Protected.
Leaving the protection policy empty (None) applies no protection, so customers can view and edit the file. It meets neither requirement.
questions.reference: Use Application Scope to protect application artifacts

questions.question:
A flow contains an If flow logic block. A Look Up Record action in the Then branch finds a record that steps after the If block also need. Referencing the action's data pill from those steps returns no value.
Which design gives the downstream steps a reliable value?
options: Set a flow variable in each branch and use the flow variable in the downstream steps
Convert the Look Up Record action into a subflow called from the If block
Add a Wait for a duration of time step after the If block
Move the downstream steps into a Do the following in parallel block
questions.explanation:
A data pill set inside the Then branch of an If block is available only to actions in the same branch, and referencing it from outside the branch produces a null value. Setting a flow variable with Set Flow Variables inside the branch, and in an Else branch when a fallback value is needed, stores the value in a flow-level data pill that the downstream steps can use.
Do the following in parallel runs actions in separate paths. It does not make data pills from the Then branch available outside that branch.
A wait delays the flow but does not change where the data pill is available. Referenced from outside the branch, it still produces a null value.
A subflow called inside the Then branch returns outputs that are also data pills set inside the branch, so they have the same limitation outside it.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug Workflow and Flow Designer

questions.question:
An automation design calls one subflow from another across multiple levels, and the last subflow in the chain calls the first one again. When the design runs, the platform stops it with an exception.
Which platform constraint does this design exceed?
options: Maximum stages per flow
Maximum number of actions per flow
Maximum triggers per flow
Indirect recursion limit
questions.explanation:
The indirect recursion limit is exceeded. The platform limits how far a chain of subflow calls can loop back on itself, through the com.glide.hub.flow_engine.indirect_recursion_limit system property. This exists to prevent runaway execution paths that could destabilize the instance. Once a chain such as Subflow A calling Subflow B calling Subflow A again exceeds that limit, the subflow call fails with an exception instead of running indefinitely.
The maximum number of actions per flow is a separate constraint from recursion. This metric counts sequential actions inside a single flow definition, not how many subflows call each other. A design can stay under the action limit and still exceed the recursion limit, because they are measuring different things.
The maximum triggers per flow rule is a design constraint, not a recursion limit. Maximum triggers per flow governs how a flow starts, not how it runs. A flow can only have one active trigger configuration, and that restriction is enforced in the trigger UI; it has nothing to do with the depth of subflow chains or publication failures caused by them.
There is no maximum stages per flow limit that would cause the described error. Maximum stages per flow does not cause run-time exceptions. Stages are progress-reporting metadata used by Service Catalog and similar interfaces; they carry no weight in execution logic or architectural validation. No platform limit on stages would stop a running flow.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug Workflow and Flow Designer

questions.question:
A record-triggered flow updates the Assignment group of Facilities Request records. The flow Run As property is set to User who initiates session. The update fails for requesters who have read-only access to the records, but it succeeds when a Developer with the admin role triggers the flow.
What explains this?
options: Record-triggered flows evaluate ACLs only for users with the admin role.
Record-triggered flows skip ACL checks when they update the triggering record.
The flow runs with the permissions of the triggering user, so ACLs block the update.
The flow runs as the System user, so ACLS apply only to the Developer's test.
questions.explanation:
With Run As set to User who initiates session, the flow's actions run with the roles of the user who triggered the flow, and access control lists (ACLs) are evaluated for that user. Requesters with read-only access cannot update the record, while the Developer with the admin role can. The Developer can run the flow as the System user or add roles with the Run with roles property.
The flow is configured to run as the user who initiates the session, not as the System user. A flow that runs as the System user is not limited by the triggering user's ACLs.
Updates from a flow that runs as the triggering user are subject to that user's ACLs, including updates to the triggering record.
ACLs are evaluated for every user. Users with the admin role usually pass them because of their role, not because ACLs are evaluated only for them.
questions.reference: Write, test, and debug Workflow and Flow Designer

questions.question: Why does the record state remain unchanged as the Flow reaches each stage?
options: Flow stages update record fields in legacy Workflow.
Stage transitions update state once the flow completes.
Flow stages are visual progress markers independent of field updates.
Stage values write to records when subflows run synchronously.
questions.explanation:
Flow stages are visual progress markers independent of field updates. In both the Flow Designer and Service Catalog contexts, Stages are purely for user feedback; they update the progress bar on a request item (RITM) or the stage field display. They do not contain logic to modify the underlying record's State (or any other) field effectively. A common developer pitfall is assuming that setting a stage named Completed naturally sets the record state to Closed Complete. It does not. Developers must explicitly add an Update Record action to change the state value in the database to match the visual stage.
Stage transitions do not update state, even after flow completion. There is no background synchronization process that aligns visual stages with data fields. The platform treats them as independent attributes. Stage state is managed by the flow engine's context, while record fields are managed by database operations. If the flow finishes without an explicit action to update the state, the record could remain in Open or Work in Progress even if the visual stage shows 100% complete. This disconnection requires deliberate configuration to resolve.
Stage values remain read-only regardless of how subflows execute. The behavior of stages is consistent across all flow configurations, whether subflows run synchronously or asynchronously. Subflows utilize the stage definitions of their parent flow (or their own, if properly mapped), but this mapping is still purely visual. Changing the execution mode of subflows does not activate a hidden write to table feature for stages. The assumption that subflow settings would alter the fundamental behavior of the stage field is incorrect; stages remain a read-only projection of flow progress, not a write-control for record data.
Flow stages do not update record fields in legacy Workflow. In reality, legacy Workflow Editor also separated Stage (visual) from State (data).
