questions.question:
A delegated developer needs a platform plugin activated for testing.
Which statement is correct?
options: Plugin activation requires admin privileges beyond delegated development.
Delegated developers can activate plugins when the plugin is listed as an app dependency.
Plugins activate automatically when referenced by a scoped app.
Delegated developers can activate plugins after a code review approval.
questions.explanation:
Plugin activation requires admin privileges beyond delegated development. It is a platform-level operation that falls outside the scope of delegated permissions. Delegated development grants permission to build and modify artifacts within assigned applications, but it does not extend to system-level operations such as activating plugins. The delegated developer must request plugin activation from an administrator. Plugins can introduce new tables, roles, and system behaviors that affect the entire instance.
Plugins do not activate automatically when referenced by a scoped app. The usage of a plugin in code or dependencies does not trigger activation. Plugin activation is always an explicit administrative action regardless of whether application code depends on plugin functionality. If a required plugin is not activated, the dependent features will fail rather than triggering automatic activation.
Delegated developers cannot activate plugins when the plugin is listed as an app dependency. Identifying a dependency in the application metadata documents the requirement but does not grant permission to satisfy it. Dependency metadata documents prerequisites for installation, but plugin activation remains a platform-level administrative action. Delegated development permissions are scoped to application artifact work and do not elevate to system operations. Even when a plugin is correctly declared as required, activation must still be performed by an administrator with the appropriate platform privileges.
Delegated developers cannot activate plugins after a code review approval. No code review workflow unlocks plugin activation for delegated developers. Plugin activation remains an admin-only operation regardless of review status. The delegated development model intentionally separates app-level development from platform-level administration. Code review gates control whether application changes are merged into the main branch, but they have no authority to escalate a developer's platform privileges or grant access to administrative functions like plugin activation.
questions.reference: Use Delegated Development to manage source code and code review

questions.question:
After several sprints a release manager finds unreviewed code in production. The team uses Delegated Development with source control integration in Studio.
Which practice failure explains this outcome?
options: Update Sets were committed to source control while in the In Progress state.
Delegated developers committed directly to the main branch in Studio.
Studio commit was executed prior to the Instance Scan suite.
Delegated developers were assigned the Manage Source Control permission.
questions.explanation:
Studio source control integration supports branch-based workflows where delegated developers create feature branches, commit changes, and submit pull requests for review before merging into the main branch. Committing directly to the main branch in Studio bypasses this review gate entirely - no pull request is created, no reviewer is assigned, and no approval occurs before changes enter the production-bound codebase. Delegated Development relies on this branching discipline to enforce code review within the Studio source control workflow.
Instance Scan execution timing relative to a Studio commit has no bearing on peer code review. Instance Scan is an automated tool that evaluates configurations against defined best-practice rules such as missing access controls, hardcoded values, or performance anti-patterns. No Instance Scan rule can assess business logic correctness, design intent, or requirement alignment. Running the scan suite before or after the commit validates configuration health, not whether a human reviewer approved the changes.
Update Set state tracks readiness for instance-to-instance promotion and operates independently from Studio source control. A delegated developer can commit to source control in Studio regardless of whether the active Update Set is In Progress or Complete. Peer review is enforced through the Studio branching and pull request workflow, not through the Update Set lifecycle. Promoting an incomplete Update Set may cause configuration gaps during instance migration, but it does not bypass the source control review process.
The Manage Source Control permission is required for delegated developers to use Studio's branching, commit, and pull request features. Granting this permission enables source control participation but does not bypass review - the permission allows developers to create branches and submit pull requests, which is the intended workflow. Review enforcement depends on whether developers use feature branches or commit directly to main, not on whether they hold the source control permission. Removing this permission would prevent delegated developers from participating in source control entirely rather than enforcing review.
questions.reference: Use Delegated Development to manage source code and code review

questions.question: Which capability statements describe delegated developer permissions for an app team?
options: Delegated developers can edit global system properties.
Delegated developers have limited privileges rather than full admin rights.
Delegated developers can build and modify artifacts within assigned apps.
Delegated developers can create new application scopes.
Delegated developers can activate platform plugins for their apps.
questions.explanation:
Delegated developers can build and modify artifacts within assigned apps. Delegated development grants designated users the ability to create and edit scripts, forms, and business rules within applications explicitly assigned to them. This is the core capability of the delegated development model, enabling non-admin developers to contribute to application development within controlled boundaries. An administrator assigns specific applications to each delegated developer, and the platform enforces scope restrictions so that developers can create and edit artifacts only within those assigned applications.
Delegated developers operate under restricted boundaries and do not receive full admin privileges. The model is designed to grant application-level development access without exposing platform-level administrative operations. This separation ensures that development work cannot affect system-wide settings or other applications. Actions such as activating plugins, creating application scopes, and modifying global system properties remain reserved for administrators, preserving instance stability while still enabling productive application development by non-admin team members.
Delegated developers cannot activate platform plugins for their apps. Plugin activation is a platform-level administrative operation that requires admin privileges. Even if a delegated developer's application depends on a specific plugin, they must request activation from an administrator rather than performing it themselves. Activating a plugin can introduce new tables, server-side logic, and system roles that impact the entire instance, which is why the platform restricts this action to administrators who can assess the broader consequences.
Delegated developers cannot create new application scopes. Creating a new application scope is an administrative action that affects the instance's application inventory. Delegated developers are limited to working within applications that have been explicitly assigned to them by an administrator. Each application scope defines a namespace and security boundary on the instance, so creating one requires administrative authority. Delegated developers work within scopes that already exist and have been assigned to their user record.
Delegated developers cannot edit global system properties. System properties are instance-wide configuration settings that affect platform behavior beyond any single application. Modifying global properties requires admin privileges, and the delegated development model intentionally excludes this capability to prevent unintended system-wide changes. Global properties control behaviors such as session timeouts, email routing, and logging levels and settings whose modification could disrupt all users and applications on the instance, not just the delegated developer's assigned app.
questions.reference: Use Delegated Development to manage source code and code review

questions.question:
A Developer commits a scoped application to a Git repository from Studio. A teammate imports the application from source control into another instance. The tables, forms, and scripts arrive, but the records in the application's Building lookup table are missing.
What explains this?
options: Source control commits data records only for administrators.
Source control excludes tables that have Allow configuration selected.
Source control commits only files tracked in a completed update set.
Source control commits application files, and lookup records are data.
questions.explanation:
Studio source control commits the application files of the application, such as tables, forms, and scripts. Records stored in the application's tables are data, so they are not committed unless the Developer adds them to the application as application files.
Source control and update sets are separate mechanisms. A commit includes the application's files regardless of the state of any update set.
Allow configuration controls whether other scopes can add configuration to a table. It does not affect what a commit includes.
The content of a commit does not depend on the user's roles. Data records are excluded for every user unless they are added as application files.

questions.question:
A Developer joins a team that keeps a scoped application in a Git repository. The application exists only in the repository and is absent from the Developer's non-production instance.
Which Studio action brings the application into the instance?
options: Import the app from source control
Link the app to source control
Create a branch
Apply remote changes
questions.explanation:
Importing an app from source control creates a new application on the instance from the remote repository. The Developer provides the repository URL, a credential with read access, and optionally a branch. Import from source control is supported only on non-production instances.
Apply remote changes pulls changes into an application that is already on the instance and linked to the repository. It does not create the application.
Linking an app to source control connects an application that already exists on the instance to a repository. The application is absent from this instance.
Creating a branch adds a branch for an application that is already linked to a repository. It does not bring the application into the instance.

questions.question: Which source control strategy prevents multiple developers from overwriting each other's changes in the same scoped application's remote repository?
options: Create a tag on the main branch before starting work
Create feature branches for isolated development
Stash local changes before committing to the main branch
Group Update Sets into batches to serialize commits
questions.explanation:
Feature branches prevent conflicts by isolating work into separate streams. Each developer works in their own branch, merging changes back to the main branch only after review and testing. This process allows conflicts to be resolved deliberately during the merge rather than occurring silently and destructively on the shared main branch.
Stashing local changes does not prevent remote conflicts when committing to the main branch. Stashing temporarily saves local work to allow context switching, but when those changes are popped and committed directly to a shared branch, the same overwrite risk exists. It is a local convenience tool, not a collaborative conflict-prevention strategy.
Grouping Update Sets does not serialize Git commits or prevent file conflicts. Update Set batching organizes changes for migration between ServiceNow instances, but source control operations (commits) happen independently of Update Set structure. Two developers committing to the same branch can still modify the same files simultaneously regardless of how their Update Sets are grouped.
Creating a tag on the main branch before starting work does not isolate development work. Tags are static markers in history used to identify specific releases or commit points (e.g., v1.0). They do not create a parallel development environment. Developers continuing to commit to the main branch after tagging will still encounter the same overwrite issues.

questions.question:
A Developer selects Apply Remote Changes in Studio and receives changes from an unexpected workstream.
What explains this outcome?
options: Apply Remote Changes pulls from the branch that received the most recent push.
The application is linked to a different branch than the Developer expected.
Apply Remote Changes merges all repository branches into the instance.
Apply Remote Changes always pulls from the default branch of the repository.
questions.explanation:
Apply Remote Changes pulls from the branch that the application currently uses. If that branch belongs to another workstream, its changes arrive on the instance. The Developer checks the current branch and switches branches before pulling.
Apply Remote Changes pulls from a single branch. Merging branches is performed in the Git service or in a local Git client.
Apply Remote Changes uses the application's current branch, which can differ from the repository's default branch.
Recent push activity on other branches does not affect the pull. The application's current branch determines the source.

questions.question:
A Developer links a scoped application to a Git repository from Studio for the first time. The repository is hosted on a public Git service.
Which two items does the Developer provide to establish the connection?
options: An update set exported from the application scope
A published version of the application in the repository
A credential with access to the repository
The URL of the remote repository
A MID Server configured for source control traffic
questions.explanation:
The repository Uniform Resource Locator (URL) identifies the remote Git repository that Studio connects to.
Studio authenticates to the Git service with a credential, such as a user name and personal access token. Without a credential that can access the repository, the connection fails.
Update sets and source control are separate mechanisms. Linking an application to Git does not use an exported update set.
A Management, Instrumentation, and Discovery (MID) Server is needed only when the repository is reachable through a private network. A repository on a public Git service is reached directly from the instance.
Publishing to the application repository is a separate distribution step. An application can be linked to Git without having been published.
